MR. GOODE  REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN NEW WESTMINSTER "COLUMBIAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. A newspaper report datelined Ottawa, May 6, and published in the Columbian of New Westminster, British Columbia, is headed "Goode moves in with Socred group". The item goes on to say this:
Tom Goode, Liberal member for Burnaby-Richmond, has moved in with the Social Credit members in the House of Commons. Goode, who shared an office on the main floor with J. A. Byrne, Kootenay East, has now moved upstairs to the sixth floor where Social Credit members and some C.C.F. are contained.

subtopic: MR. GOODE  REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN NEW WESTMINSTER "COLUMBIAN"
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MR. GOODE  REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN NEW WESTMINSTER "COLUMBIAN"
speechtext:
This is a most serious matter to me, Mr. Speaker. After listening to my statements I hope that my friends will also consider it to be serious. The article continues:
Liberals are housed on the ground floor and third floor, Conservatives and some C.C.F. are on the fourth and fifth floors and Social Credit, some independents and C.C.F. are in offices on the top floor.
Goode, who has served on the government's standing committee on external affairs, has been replaced on that body by Maurice Boisvert, Nicolet-Yamaska.
Mr. Speaker, the statement has no substance whatever in truth. I do not need to tell you that the office arrangements listed in the article are entirely wrong. I have had an office on the sixth floor of this building since 50433-225
the first of this parliament. I share that office with the Liberal member for Papineau (Mr. Meunier), and I am most happy with those arrangements. Alongside of me are ten other Liberal members of parliament, each of whom, because of the arrangement, could be accused of joining another party. I think the house will agree that the statement which I have read to you is an example of yellow journalism at its very lowest. It has always been my impression in this house that legislation has been suggested from opposition parties which I could support, because in my view it would build towards national unity and was for the betterment of the Canadian people. I propose to continue that course.
This article has been printed by an irresponsible newspaper and I have been assured that no member of the press gallery in Ottawa sent the article to the west. Nothing but contempt can be held for a paper whose policy would direct that an article of this kind should appear on its pages. I challenge the Columbian in New Westminster to prove that this article is correct, and I challenge them to name their Ottawa correspondent. The people of my riding will know how to deal with such a contemptible political move.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY IN MEETING OF NATO COUNCIL
PARTICIPATION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY IN MEETING OF NATO COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members would not like to see pass unnoticed in the records of the house the significance of the participation for the first time of the representatives of the Federal Republic of Germany in the meeting of the North Atlantic council in Paris today. Perhaps I might be allowed to read into the record the statement made in that connection on behalf, I am sure, of all members of the house and of the people of Canada generally on the importance of that event. It is as follows:
The historic significance of this council meeting is apparent to us all. The German Federal Republic, as a result of agreements freely concluded, and which have been approved by our legislatures, now becomes a member of NATO- an organization devoted solely to international peace,

NATO Council Meeting
security and welfare. We warmly welcome Chancellor Adenauer as the first representative of Germany to our council, and as a man who has already proven his devotion to the ideals we share.
We are here also to examine in confidence and frankness the international situation, particularly in the light of recent developments. That situation, at least in Europe, has improved. This gives us reason for satisfaction, but none for abandoning those policies which have to a large extent been responsible for that improvement.
This council meeting marks the successful completion of long and patient effort by those around this table and by others who are no longer with us on the council to broaden and strengthen the basis of our NATO association.
It marks also a new phase in the development of both European unity and the Atlantic community. France and Germany, not because they forget" but because they remember the past, have come together in a western European union which includes Italy, Belgium. The Netherlands, Luxembourg and also Great Britain whose vision across the seas has not prevented the acceptance of a new and indispensable European role. Europe, however, even a uniting Europe, is not enough, and NATO, the vigorous and hopeful expression of the Atlantic idea, is recognition of that fact.
NATO is growing stronger and free Germany adds to that strength. This strength is, however, merely a means to an end, international peace and security. Therefore we must exploit every genuine opportunity to seek by negotiation solutions for the problems which tcday keep alive fears and tensions in the world.
This remains our most important NATO task. Only strength and steadiness will see it through .to a successful conclusion.
All these things have been said so often by so many so much better than I have been able to do that I feel almost apologetic for repeating the obvious. I am, however, grateful for the 'opportunity to reaffirm, and on an occasion of such momentous importance, the loyalty of the government and people of my country to the ideals of peaceful and fruitful co-operation which inspire this great Atlantic organization, into which we now welcome our German colleagues. The developments which have culminated in this meeting give us greater reason for faith and confidence in the future.
X am sure we all share that faith and confidence in the future and we all hope that France and Germany will not have to forget but rather will remember the past to make effective and lasting their united efforts to further peace and happiness in the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY IN MEETING OF NATO COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be appropriate that I should say a few words with regard to the statement the Prime Minister has placed on the record concerning this extremely important event that has taken place today. It is in fact one of the most unique events in history. It comes on the tenth anniversary of V-E day. It comes on the tenth anniversary of a time when our forces were discovering the full horrors of Dachau, Buchenwald, Belsen and those other camps of terror. Let us never forget this because the things that happened there are things with respect to which our purpose must 
always be the prevention of any repetition of human suffering of that kind.
Remembering these things, we will have a firmer basis for the grounds of friendship that have emerged on this tenth anniversary of the day when Germany surrendered. Chancellor Adenauer said today that Germany had paid the price of the terrible leadership to which the people had submitted. He could say that because he was one man who paid a price himself for opposing personally the evil forces that Hitler had let loose. Chancellor Adenauer also said in his remarks today, and I thought these words were memorable, that from this dreadful punishment Germany had emerged cleansed and purified and that the German people were ready to go forward recognizing the price of leadership of the kind from which they had suffered.
It seems to me this is a day to remember the things that have happened but it is also a day for great hope. As we welcome Germany into the western fellowship, I think we should also pay our tribute to France which, with all the millions of graves to remind her of German aggression, has welcomed in terms of friendship an enemy of so short a time ago. France has more reason than any other nation in the world to be conscious of what German aggression means. This day can be one of the turning points of history. This can well become one of the most memorable dates that people will recall centuries from now if the spirit of that great German, Chancellor Adenauer, continues to guide the German people in the years ahead.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gregg for the second reading of Bill No. 328, respecting unemployment insurance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other evening when the minister moved second reading of the bill, we had had it in our hands for some considerable time. We have now had the bill for something over a month. I suppose if we had it for a year we would still see in it something that had previously escaped our notice.
Since it is the duty of the official opposition to inquire into the provisions of any legislation presented to the house, there are a few things I would like to bring to the minister's attention. It is true that we shall have the opportunity to examine the measure clause by clause when it is placed before the standing committee on industrial relations. However, there are one or two points I should like to make at this time.
This bill proposes amendments which will have a serious effect on the administration of the act. Some of the provisions of the bill are rather wide in their scope. For one thing, up to the present time insured persons have been educated to the daily contribution basis of making contributions to the fund. They will now have to be re-educated to the weekly contribution basis. Members in the house will be interested to know just what plans the department has made for this change-over.
I recall very well that when the Unemployment Insurance Act first came into being there was an extensive educational program, involving regional conferences, where employers and employees were instructed as to the effects of the act, and representatives of commerce and industry had laid down to

them the manner in which they must proceed to insure their employees. I was at two or three of these conferences myself and I recall the time which was spent in instructing employers generally with respect to the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Now that the basis of contribution is changed rather radically, I wonder what provision the minister has made for re-educating people who have become so used to the old system of daily contributions.
As I said at the resolution stage and again the other evening, Mr. Speaker, the members of this group are opposed to the reduction in the maximum benefit period from 51 weeks to 30 weeks. If I recall the minister's remarks correctly, and if he claimed that only 3 [DOT] 5 per cent of payments were paid for the maximum period, a matter with which I would like to deal at a later stage, then I fail to see why it was necessary to reduce the maximum period, as is now suggested. I am not using particularly as an argument the fact that only 3-5 per cent were paid for the maximum period because, in my opinion, the matter must be viewed from the standpoint of the rights of the individual rather than from the impact which such action would have on the fund.
I might also draw attention to the fact that contribution rates have likewise been raised, notably in the case of those workers who are in the higher wage bracket and who have more continuity of employment and consequently are not so apt to benefit. I might say in this regard, Mr. Speaker, that persons over the age of 60 years, let us say, have received a relatively high proportion of the total benefit days paid. For instance, such persons received in the calendar year 1953 a total of 8,125,160 benefit days or 18-2 per cent, out of a total benefit days paid of 44,660,188. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that elderly people-I would not have the temerity to call a person 60 years of age elderly, but those persons who have passed 60, let me say-are more likely to be eligible for the maximum duration of regular benefits. Retired persons would therefore constitute a group most likely, in my opinion, to be affected by the reduction in the maximum benefit period.
Much has been made of the new classifications in the act, under the new rates of contribution and benefits. I should like to draw attention to the fact that in the top bracket the employee and the employer alike are now supposed to pay 60 cents a week as against the old maximum of 54 cents a week, so that there is an additional contribution of 12 cents per employee per week. Added to that is the government's share of the contribution, which means that the fund will benefit to the
Unemployment Insurance Act extent of approximately 15 cents a week per employee for those persons who are in the highest contribution bracket. Despite those additional contributions, the claimant will actually receive considerably less than he would have received at the old rate. At the old rate he would have received 51 weeks' benefit of $24 a week, a total of $1,224. Under the new scheme he will receive 30 weeks' benefit, at $30 a week, or a total of $900. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that I am not dealing at the moment with supplerrientary benefits, or with what now would be called seasonal benefits.
In other classifications maximum benefits under the new act are in excess of $300 less than those obtainable under the old act. I hold in my hand some calculations which have been made, and I find that persons who are now in the $35 a week class of earnings actually will receive $441 less under the new act, or actually could receive as a maximum benefit $441 less under the new act than they could have received under the old act. At $30 a week they will receive $378 less, and even at $50 a week they will receive $414 less than they could have received as maximum benefit under the old act. Of course, those calculations are based on just what information is available to us. For instance, under the amendments which are being made to the act, the regulations under which those seasonal benefits will now be administered are still a mystery to us. As a matter of fact, until the commission has made the regulations which it is entitled to make under the provisions of these amendments, none of us will know precisely what the seasonal benefits will amount to, nor how they are to be administered.
With regard to the contributions which I referred to a moment ago which will be made to the fund, I have taken the figures which appear in the Labour Gazette for April, 1955, showing estimates of the insured population under the Unemployment Insurance Act. These figures appear on page 483 under table E-4. There I find that in December of 1954, the last month for which figures are available, there were 3,275,000 persons insured under the Unemployment Insurance Act. If we estimate that 50 per cent of these people are in the top contribution bracket- and I think that is, if anything, a little on the low side because the last figures which are available to us are for 1951, four years ago, when there were 47 [DOT] 39 per cent in the top insured bracket, and everyone knows how wages have increased since then-we find in the last report which is available for unemployment and payrolls, the average weekly wage for Canada as of February 1, 1955, was
3568	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance Act $60.12, and the employees reported numbered nearly 2,500,000. As a matter of fact, with the exception of four provinces, all provinces reported their averages as considerably above the maximum mentioned in the provisions of the new act. If then we tend to be a little on the conservative side and take only 50 per cent of the insured population as a reasonable number, and calculate the amount of the additional contribution which will be paid by this 50 per cent from employer and employee and the government's contribution, we shall find that in one year, even if the number of insured persons does not increase, the additional contributions to the fund will be something of the nature of $13 million. As a matter of fact, just on those figures which I have quoted, I make it $12,772,500 additional contributions to the fund from that class of workers in the coming year. Far from being a drain on the fund, this class of worker, who over the years has been the backbone of the fund, who has contributed more to the fund than any other class, will continue to contribute a great deal more than any other individual class.
I would think it might be well for us to consider again this maximum period; rather than to cut the maximum period for benefits we should find jobs for these people. Employed persons are not a drain on the fund; quite the reverse, they are the people who build it up. Those people who tend to lose most from this deal which is proposed in the amendments are those persons who have given, and who will continue to give, the most to the fund.
I should like also to make some remarks with reference to permissible earnings. I hope that when we are in committee the minister will be able to tell us just what type of thinking prompted the limitation on a man earning from $6 or $8 a week to earning no more than an additional $2 a week while the man who receives $30 a week is to be allowed $13 a week in addition. Under the old act and regardless of the benefit classification a man was permitted to earn up to $2 a day which frequently amounted to some $14 a week and in the majority of cases amounted to about $12 a week.
It is almost impossible to determine the intent of some of the sections of this bill without knowing what regulations are likely to be put into effect. I have mentioned already the difficulty that we have had trying to discover just what the benefits are likely to be for those persons who qualify for seasonal benefits, particularly if they are in the class of persons to which I have referred, those who have been retired from business but who still apply for employment.
[Mrs. Fairclough.l
I notice instances where conditions governing rights are described merely as being subject to such regulations as may be prescribed by the commission. I suppose we shall not know for some time just what those regulations will be. How can we know whether the provisions of the act will meet the situation if such provisions are limited by phrases such as the one I have mentioned?
In my remarks at the resolution stage I referred to the necessity of evolving some plan to cover fishermen. I had rather hoped that when the amendments were available in bill form we would find that this matter had been taken care of. However, on going over the amendments very carefully I find that there has been no inclination to cover this class of worker. I strongly urge the minister and his officials to undertake such planning without delay because now that we are coming into the summer season we should be making plans to cover people who are likely to be affected when cold weather strikes us once more.
I must say that I am disappointed in the various sections which deal with the setting up of committees. Even in the description of the personnel of the commission there is no reference to the inclusion of women either on the commission or on the committees. I feel most strongly that there should be a woman commissioner. I have spoken on this matter before in this house, on the estimates and when we were considering amendments to the act, and I once again draw to the attention of the minister the fact that no provision has been made for the appointment of a woman commissioner.
I think this should be done even though it means the enlargement of the commission by one person. I believe also that the advisory committee and the national employment committee should likewise have women members. It would appear to be a simple thing to stipulate this in the redrafting of the act. I hope that when the matter is before the committee the minister will show an inclination to consider this point and make the necessary amendments to put it into effect.
Speaking of the commission and the rules which govern the appointment of commissioners, I must say that one is led to wonder why the government, which has expended such large sums of money and such a tremendous amount of eloquence in advocating that older workers should not be retired on the ground of chronological age while still physically and mentally fit to perform the duties of their office, should now reduce the eligible service age of commissioners from 70 years, as specified in the old act, to the 65 years now prescribed in the revision.

With regard to the composition of the boards of referees, again I submit that there should be women on these boards. When I make that comment I am thinking of the substantial percentage of appellants to the boards of referees who are women. I am sure that those members of the minister's department who are thoroughly experienced in this field will agree with me that a large percentage of appellants are women and consequently there should be women appointed to these boards of referees.
I cannot find either that the new bill makes any reference to veterans other than in one small instance. Undoubtedly there will be problems affecting those who are presently in European service and those who have returned from Korea. There is no section of the act as it now stands which permits special service to these men. I should like very much to know just how the commission proposes to handle their cases and whether they are to be given any special consideration, consideration which I think they deserve because of their long absence from this country.
In the explanatory notes which appear at the beginning of the act it is noted that one of the objectives was the rearrangement of the sections and parts of the act to bring them into context with other sections of related nature and to clarify the text. At first study it appears to me that the rearrangement consists in substantial measure in the elimination of those clauses which are difficult to administer, and again I cite the old sections Nos. 101 to 107 dealing with veterans. I realize that some of the provisions relating to veterans are no longer required in connection with those particular workers, but undoubtedly those sections were difficult to administer. Then there are the sections dealing with short-time claimants and others of a like nature.
In my estimation the general tenor of the revisions has been bureaucratic in the extreme. Apparently anything which irritates the administration must be dealt with. As I said the other evening, nothing has brought this attitude to my mind so emphatically as the minister's reference to what he termed interim arrangements. On looking up my previous remarks I find that I referred to this on April 26 as reported on page 3202 of Hansard. I should like to place my words once more on the record, and they are:
The minister referred a few moments ago to an interim arrangement which would take care of those persons who have had their benefits drastically curtailed by the reduction which is contemplated, from 51 weeks to 30 weeks. He used a few words in describing these people which brought home to me, even more forcibly than an examination of the bill had done, just how far 50433-226
Unemployment Insurance Act
the thinking of the government and the commission has gone along the lines of a bureaucratic approach to the administration of this act.
I have already mentioned the elimination of the clauses dealing with veterans and with short-term claimants. In addition, right through the act there is the tendency to substitute the word "is" for the former words "may be". There is also a tightening up of the time element with reference to appeals. In many instances where 60 days, 90 days or 6 months were allowed, the new act stipulates that 30 days only will be allowed.
As I examined this act I was amazed at the number of instances where I found the words "is final and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court". In the old act, Mr. Speaker, I can find only one circumstance which prohibits appeal to the civil courts, but in the new act there are a number of them; there are at least half a dozen and probably more. I am not a lawyer, but as a layman I fail to understand how it can happen that a body corporate which can sue or be sued can inaugurate legislation which deprives citizens of their inalienable right of impartial hearing and judicial decision as to whether the citizen's views or those of the commission shall prevail. I find this to be a step in the wrong direction. Once more we slide towards the bureaucratic philosophy. In any other group such provisions would be met with the charge of calculated lawlessness. In this group, where the backing of the government is behind those who propose these changes, I must admit that I can hardly think of a term with which to describe the tendency.
I should like to draw attention to the problems which face administrators of this act. Probably the main point which immediately assails the eye, on perusing the statistical data which are available, is that the average period of unemployment has been lengthening each year. I refer to the recently published reference paper No. 58, entitled "The Labour Force", which covers the period of the last ten years and which just came to my desk the other day. From this report and from the reports which I have received since January from the bureau of statistics, I find these interesting facts.
In January of this year there were 23,000 persons who had been looking for work for between seven and twelve months. When I speak about the term of seven to twelve months, Mr. Speaker, I should like the members of this house to recall that these are the people who are going to be affected by this reduction from 51 weeks to 30 weeks. There were 23,000 of those people in January of this year as against less than 10,000 in January of 1954; in fact, in every January reported for the last ten years there were less

Unemployment Insurance Act than 10,000. In February of this year we had
26,000	persons reported as seeking work for more than seven months. Last year in February we had 13,000. The year before we had less than 10,000, and that record goes back for several years. In March of this year we had 31,000 people seeking work for more than seven months. Last year in March we had 17,000. There were nearly twice as many this year. The year before that we had less than 10,000 and so on. The picture is pretty much the same. Going back to 1950, which now seems a long time ago, I see that there were 20,000 in that year also. However, in 1954 as the season progressed right up until the end of June, these figures with regard to persons seeking work for more than seven months gradually increased; and if the same pattern is followed this year we can expect that the figure for those persons seeking work for a period of seven to twelve months will have increased in 1955 as it did in 1954.
I do not know whether that is the reason that the government has decided to cut these off from benefits. I do not know whether they have decided that, since there are so many more who are seeking work for a longer period of time, they must refuse to them the benefits to which they are entitled under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I should not like to think that. I hope that, when we come to the consideration of these individual clauses, it will turn out that there has been some other thinking which prompted that action. But whether or not that was the reason, Mr. Speaker, that is the result. There are more and more people each year who are unemployed for longer and longer periods of time. I do not intend to put on the record any more statistics in this regard, but I refer hon. members to this copy of "The Labour Force", page 67, table 11, from which they can see that the same situation applies to all of the applicants. In the four to six months' period looking for work they will find that the numbers have substantially increased.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that we have a special problem in the winter months. It is a problem which has been recognized by everyone who has examined unemployment insurance and the causes of unemployment. As winter is a formidable foe in warfare, I think it would be well if we considered that it is also a formidable foe in employment. Thinking along these lines, I recall the time when Sir Winston Churchill, the prime minister of the United Kingdom, was speaking of the alibi which Hitler had given to his people for the losses in the winter campaign. Sir Winston Churchill said, "He found out they have winter in Russia", a very elemental lesson, and one that Napoleon also learned.
fMrs. Fairclough.]

I suggest that it is about time this government found out that we have winter in Canada every year.
Every year the figures with regard to unemployment have increased over the last few years until this year on March 19-the date for which we received the highest figures on applications for employment-they had reached the staggering figure of 633,000. I do not wonder that those persons who are charged with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act should feel a little bit nervous about this situation. But after all, Mr. Speaker, unemployment insurance is, at best, only a palliative. Undoubtedly it has saved us this year from a major crisis but I urge the minister to get busy now to make plans for employment, not for unemployment. I urge that he do not sit back and wait for the report from the new royal commission on economic prospects. You will not have that report for at least two years, and that means two more winters that we must go through before we can even find out what the findings of that commission will be. Spring is the time, in my estimation, for the start of an investigation into and assessment of the situation with which we are faced. I noticed a Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa in the Hamilton Spectator of last Saturday headed, "Jobless Figures Falling Faster, Officials Claim". The article reads in part as follows:
However, present Information indicates that the number of jobless still is numerically higher than at the same time last year.
Apparently it is a matter for some elation that the figures as to jobless are falling despite the fact that we still have more people unemployed than at the same time last year. The article continues:
One of the reasons for this, the informant said, is that employment has not kept pace with a growth of 100,000 in the labour force.
If that is true, if that is the reason, then I would think it is all the more reason why the minister should be considering seriously what he is going to do about the winter of 1955-56. Now that the unemployment figures are falling, as this press release indicates, now when an inquiry into the causes of the circumstances surrounding unemployment could scarcely be termed traitorous, as was the allegation almost against those persons who did make some inquiries into it, now in the spring when everyone feels a little hopeful we might take an objective view of the whole employment picture not merely to determine the number of people who are without work but in order to make a careful study of the steps necessary to provide the maximum of employment for the workers of this country.

It is no use to procrastinate until a crisis is upon us. In this regard the government has acted very much like the lazy man with the leaky roof. When it was raining hard he could not get up on the roof to repair it and when it was not raining it did not leak, so he just let it go. I was very much interested to read in a recent issue of the Fundy Fisherman some remarks with which I should like to close these few comments. In doing so, I urge once more upon the minister careful consideration of the criticisms that have been made of these amendments, and in particular some action with regard to unemployment. The editorial commences by saying:
Unemployment In any country Is not only a useless luxury but a terrific waste which no nation can really afford.
After further pertinent remarks, the editorial concludes in this way:
But, to accept unemployment in Canada as something of a chronic condition is both unwise and unnecessary; and unworthy of a strong and vigorous people that has a mighty task ahead in building up the nation to become one of the truly great nations of the world.
I hope that all the way through the consideration of the bill we can keep these views before us and that we will judge these amendments not only from the standpoint of expediency or the ease with which the act can be administered by the officials but also from the very human aspect of what it is that is needed in the country to give employment to our people and how best the government can serve the workers of Canada.

I have always done the kind of thing I am doing now. I have always tried to make sensible proposals with respect to the unemployed in order to enable them to get food, clothing and shelter. I never did consider it a subject for propaganda. It should not be used as such. That is the great difficulty. There are so many people who pay lip service to the problem but refuse to face up to it and find a solution by making changes. You cannot cure unemployment by carrying on as we have carried on since 1867, that is by getting the occasional war to relieve it and then returning to a condition of unemployment as soon as this supply and demand formula fails.
As I said in the beginning, I am not going into all the ramifications of this bill. The bill is going to a committee where it will be studied clause by clause. Before the committee studies the bill we are going to have the benefit of the opinion of the two labour congresses, who have been studying it for some considerable time. We shall also, I hope, have the benefit of the views of the manufacturers association, who will give us the other side of the story. Any specific criticisms I have to make concerning this bill I shall hold until I have the benefit of these discussions. Then, when the bill is before the committee, we will study it section by section.
I should like to say this for the benefit of the minister. Since we received the bill we have looked at it and have done some work on it ourselves as a committee of our caucus. We have talked to some people about the bill. Before the bill is finally passed, there is one change about which I feel the minister should think and that is the change from 51 weeks to 30 weeks of benefits. As the minister himself pointed out during the course of his presentation, actually only about 4 per cent of the recipients of unemployment insurance are affected. If there are only 3 per cent or 4 per cent affected, the cost is not very great and I do not see any reason for the change. If 3 per cent or 4 per cent of the recipients of unemployment insurance are going to lose out by this change from 51 weeks to 30 weeks, then I feel the minister should consider continuing the old section of the act.
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
The next point I should like the minister to consider is the change in the categories. Something has been done about it. A couple of additional categories have been created. About 43 per cent of those now covered by unemployment insurance will fit into the ceiling of $57, but I think there should be another category from $57 tew at least $63. There are a great many employees, particularly in the building trades, who make up to $100 per week. Now, these people are seasonal employees and by making $57 the top bracket those who earn much more than that will suffer. I am thinking of those in the building trades, the automobile industry, and there are categories in other industries in which the wages are much higher than that. I feel the minister should consider establishing another category from $57 to around $63 or higher if he so desires. I think he should take a look at that particular problem.
I am disappointed also that regulation 5A, section 35, of the act, still remains there. This is the beartrap to which I referred when I spoke at the resolution stage, under which married women are penalized. Everyone with whom I have talked about that particular section, both in and out of the house, thinks it should be removed. It is an administrative headache, anyway. I know that in my own part of the country the board of referees would like to have it removed because the case of every married woman who makes application finally gets into their hands, and it is a headache.
The supplementary benefits also require looking over, I believe. Those who receive supplementary benefits under unemployment insurance year by year are the seasonal workers. In this country the seasonal workers make up about 25 per cent of the working force. The change that is being made now in that particular section will cause suffering to a lot of people. These are the ones who are obliged to go the full term under the act, then take supplementary benefits, and finally even those run out and they are totally unemployed. I believe we will have to take a good look at that. In my judgment the act should provide that any person who is unemployed should receive unemployment insurance until such time as he is gainfully employed; that has always been my conception of an unemployment insurance act. Unless it does that, it is not serving the purpose it was intended to serve.
There is another matter about which I should like the minister to think. I do not know whether he can do anything about it except consult with the Department of National Defence. The Canadian Legion made a proposal to the veterans affairs committee

when we were considering the Veterans Benefit Act a week or so ago. At the moment service personnel are covered if they are in the special force in Germany or Korea. Service personnel in the regular forces are covered up to July of this year. Any person who enlists in the regular army for a period of five years or seven years will not be covered for unemployment purposes after July of this year. The Legion recommended that the committee should consider the possibility of bringing all service personnel under unemployment insurance on a contributory basis.
We discussed this proposal at considerable length and reported to the defence department that consideration should be given to it. There are men who will enlist in the regular forces for three years, five years or seven years and after they are in for a couple of years they discover they just cannot go through with it and make the armed forces their vocation. There are many reasons for that. These people find themselves coming out of the service after three or four years, with no right to unemployment insurance. While I am not committed in my own mind one way or the other, I think this is a problem that is going to develop after July of this year. The veterans affairs committee referred the matter to the Department of National Defence, requesting them to conduct a poll of opinion in the services as to whether or not service personnel wanted unemployment insurance on a contributory basis. I believe the Minister of Labour should consult with the Minister of National Defence and get the officers of their department who have training in that field to take a look at the matter. The Legion was rather strongly in favour of insurance for the regular forces on a contributory basis after July of this year.
As I said when I began, Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of going over all the things I said at the resolution stage. I am going to conclude my remarks at this point, Mr. Speaker, and shall wait for the committee stage to discuss it clause by clause.

Once that is done, immediately industry will begin to produce more goods and create jobs, without any force being used. The demand will be there, and the jobs will be forthcoming.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said, in effect: "Well, this unemployment problem is not so great that it could not be solved by a little war." Of course the hon. member was not suggesting that we should have a war; but the cold, hard fact is that in this country, under a Liberal or a Conservative government, we have never been able to solve our problem of unemployment until war came along and did it for us. There is no use hanging our heads and saying, "Well, that is not the way to talk. You are talking war, and that is a lot of silly nonsense". But when we look at the cold, hard fact we see that that is the only way our unemployment has ever been solved.
When I say to the minister that probably his department is wrongly named, there may be some merit in my suggestion. If the Minister of Labour had the job of creating conditions to defeat unemployment I believe he would show results, because he has shown great interest in the problem. I do not know of any minister who has held his portfolio who has shown greater sympathy and interest. I know the late Mr. Mitchell was highly respected in the house, but I do not think his enthusiasm or desire went beyond that of the minister now in office.
But he has an impossible task, because the government has failed to recognize this economic principle reflected in a lack of purchasing power. Then when unemployment comes along as a result of the government's policy the condition is thrown on the doorstep of the Minister of Labour, and he is told, "Get these guys jobs". It just cannot be done by any unemployment program.
I do not have to be a prophet when I say it cannot be done that way. There can be no doubt that unemployment insurance is a good thing, and I believe the minister is trying to do all he can to patch up an old and outmoded method of financing. I wish him
tMr. Johnston (Bow River).]
the best of luck, but I think his efforts are not going to achieve the results he would like to see.
There are some things in the bill about which I am not too fussy. I am glad the act is going to have a general revision. Since its inception in 1941 this will be the first. To deal in greater detail, I do not care particularly for section 52 which carries the marginal notation, "Only one period between December 1st and April 15th". I believe if we are going to have unemployment insurance it should be made applicable to an individual whenever he is unemployed. If an insured happens to receive his benefits within that stated period of time, no matter how short the time may be, he is limited to that one period. If individuals are to pay their contributions into an insurance fund, then it should be truly an insurance fund, and whenever an occasion arises the individual should receive assistance.
As I indicated at the outset of my remarks, I do not think this is the proper time to discuss details of the bill. If I began discussing the clauses I would no doubt be called to order, and quite properly so. Speaking generally, I believe the minister is endeavouring to make an improvement in this instance. At the committee stage we shall take advantage of the opportunities presented to us to discuss the measure clause by clause. Therefore, with that in mind, I shall leave any further remarks I might have to the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I assure the house my remarks will be brief, and I say to the minister that my expressions of disappointment will not be as numerous as those indicated by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). My observations will be limited to one clause in the bill.
In spite of views expressed this afternoon, I am convinced that the labour force in Canada will receive with great satisfaction this measure to amend and to consolidate the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) must be congratulated on introducing this measure which will strengthen further the purposes of the act and make it more effective as an insurance policy protecting our working class. I am particularly interested in the application of this act to fishermen and on this point I wish to quote remarks made by the Minister of Labour when he spoke on the introduction of the resolution. I quote from page 2714 of Hansard of April 5:
I have not given up hope that we may find a solution. I know it will not be a perfect solution but I hope we can find a good solution

somewhere, whether it comes within the field of unemployment insurance, under some special measure administered by the Department of Fisheries, or a combination of both.
I am rather disappointed, however, that no decision has been reached to date during the present session with regard to extending unemployment insurance to fishermen. I am prepared to admit that such a proposal poses some very difficult problems from an unemployment insurance standpoint, but situations offering similar or just as serious objections have been given consideration and dealt with to the satisfaction of the labour class concerned.
In April of 1951 the unemployment commission issued a report of a survey of the fishing industry and concluded its summarized recommendations with the following, as found on page 82, paragraph 279, of the report of the survey of the fishing industry in Canada by coverage division of the insurance branch. I wish to quote this paragraph from the report:
If it is necessary to augment the income derived by fishermen from fishing, subsistence farming and other employment, some form of unemployment assistance should be provided by the proper authorities rather than attempting to strain the framework of unemployment insurance to take care of a situation that is not properly an insurance function.
It is therefore recommended that the exception of employment in fishing be continued.
I have given a complete and serious study to this report, Mr. Speaker, and particularly to the section dealing with the gulf of St. Lawrence area. For this study this area covered the fishing industry of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, the Magdalen islands and the Gaspe peninsula. According to the said report, in the area covered, 19,800 fishermen are engaged in inshore fishing and 560 in deep-sea fishing. Of these 20,000 fishermen over half, or 11,000, are from New Brunswick. In dealing with inshore fishing the report states that approximately 83 per cent of the fishermen are working on shares, which is about correct. However, on page 25 of the report dealing with deep-sea fishing I find the following statement:
The home of deep-sea fishing in this area is in Gloucester county in New Brunswick. The deep-sea fishing force is about 560 fishermen. The survey covered 17 vessels or 17 per cent of the total vessels in this group. These vessels fish on the New Brunswick banks, or on the north shore banks. They are owned in the proportion of about 55 per cent by fishing firms or fish buyers and 45 per cent by one member of the crew, generally the master. The equipment is owned by the owner of the vessel.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, to have to admit that I cannot agree with this statement, which is not entirely according to facts. No fishing firm in Gloucester county, handling deep-sea
9, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act fish, has any ownership or share in the existing fishing fleet. This deep-sea fleet, now consisting of over 60 draggers and a number of smaller vessels, is owned exclusively by individuals or by groups of fishermen who are the sole owners of their vessels.
It appears that of the total fishing force of
88.000	men in Canada, only 6,000 are wage earners; over 18,000 are loan workers and
63.000	are working on shares as working owners or as members of the crew. I realize that it may not be possible or logical to insure the owners of fishing vessels, but it seems to me that a solution could be arrived at by which wage earners and fishermen fishing on shares would be granted the privilege of unemployment insurance benefits. The share received by these fishermen, be it on a daily or on a weekly basis, is considered as the total amount of their salary or wages based on the total quantity and value of the fish landed. There is, in fact, very little difference and much similarity between the earnings of a person working in a factory being paid on piece work and the earnings of a fisherman deriving his salary from the proceeds of the fish catch landed.
I cannot agree with, and I must take exception to, the decision or recommendation of the unemployment commission report following its 1951 survey which I quoted earlier in my remarks. I cannot agree with the conclusion that some form of unemployment assistance should be provided by the proper authorities rather than attempting to strain the framework of unemployment insurance to take care of a situation that is not properly an insurance function. Whether it be the inshore fishermen spending two or three months of the year at lobster or herring fishing, whether it be the deep-sea fishermen engaged in New Brunswick at least from May to November and fishing on a share basis, these men are part of our labour force and are entitled to the benefits of this great insurance scheme instituted for the protection and welfare of our Canadian working class. Their employment is no more seasonal than that of the carpenter who has to lay off work during the winter season on account of the drastic cut in construction work, or the longshoreman who has to wait for the opening of the shipping season in the spring before resuming his work.
I realize that problems will arise with respect to the collection of contributions and the control and the administration of the act if it applies to fishermen. Some arbitrary rules may have to be enacted to determine when a fisherman becomes unemployed, but, Mr. Speaker, in most cases a fisherman is not

Unemployment Insurance Act working for himself and a certain contract of service does exist between him and the vessel owners.
Paragraph 278 of the report of the survey previously mentioned states:
It is hard to see how. under these circumstances, the extension of unemployment insurance to the fishing industry would be any advantage to most of the persons engaged in it, whether they were wage earners or share fishermen.
Here again, Mr. Speaker, I must take exception to and I cannot agree with the conclusion arrived at by the commission. We have in this country a certain group or proportion of our labour class which is known as or could be called a diversified labour group. The majority of our fishermen could easily be classified as part of this group. Let us take as an example the helper of a herring and lobster fisherman along the Northumberland strait area. From four to five weeks in the spring he is engaged in herring fishing and for two months, August and September, he is back again to help a boat owner with his lobster operations. In October he is out to the lumber camps to help in the annual cut of pulpwood, pit props or long lumber. Early in January this man is back home again after the closing of the camps which have completed their quota for the year. During this short period of employment this man has not paid enough unemployment insurance daily contributions to claim benefits for his period of unemployment from January to April. If this same man had been allowed to contribute under this act during this period of fishing in the spring and late summer, he could now qualify for benefits, and his family would not suffer the hardships and privations faced by a large number of similar cases along our entire fishing districts. Similar situations exist all along the shore of my constituency of Gloucester and in many other sections of the maritimes. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that the present act still offers the possibility for the unemployment insurance commission to reconsider its decision and include a certain number of our fishermen under insurance benefits.
The immense fishing resources of Canada have contributed substantially to the general economy of our country and its considerable expansion is still of paramount importance to the coastal provinces where commercial fishing is pursued on a large scale. Canada after all leads the world in the export of its fishing products. Are we going to allow this industry to be curtailed in its expansion by penalizing the primary producers, those hardworking fishermen to whom a 44 to 48 hour week is a thing unknown? Are we going to
[Mr. Robichaud.l

endanger this expanding industry by refusing to these fishermen the security offered in other working fields?
In conclusion I urge that during this present session the Minister of Labour insist upon the unemployment insurance commission reconsidering its decision and giving further consideration to the adoption of a system which would qualify at least a certain class or type of fishermen under the unemployment insurance benefits.

First, there came a large expense for psychiatric treatment for one of the adolescent children, a heavy medical expense. Then followed a prolonged period of unemployment.
Then followed the family's ejection from a rented property. To find shelter for a family of seven children it was necessary to purchase a home. Today the father lives with one relative, the wife and baby live with another relative, and friends have taken in the other children in order that a home may be found for them.
Here is case No. 2, also provided by the Toronto branch of the same association. In the family are the father, mother and four children. The father was laid off work last fall; no unemployment insurance was available because of lack of sufficient days. The welfare department of the city of Toronto helped the family out for a week or two. The Salvation Army provided some relief. Neighbours did what they could. The family were eventually driven to such straits that the father applied to the children's aid society and asked the children's aid to place his children in homes because they were going hungry and he could not provide for them. The children's aid society assured him that, as a respectable citizen, it was his duty to provide for the children and that they could not, under the circumstances, place them in homes. Eventually the landlord, whose rent had been getting in arrears, served eviction notice. The day the notice was received, the father walked out and has not been heard from since.
As to case No. 3, this man had been unemployed for six months. At first he was optimistic; he would get a job even though others could not. When this effort failed, he decided he would go into business for himself, selling silverware from door to door. By Christmastime he had to give it up; it was no go. The family was desperate. He became irritable and quarrelsome, his face thin and white. Finally his wife got work. He stayed home to cook. He took the children to the nursery as their mother used to do. As the weeks went by he became more ill-tempered. He began to slap his children for little provocation. He has developed a bad cough and looks sicker and sicker as
fMr. Noseworthy.]
the days roll by. When this man was gainfully employed, the social worker says, he was a happy, useful citizen. Today he is despondent, sick and dependent on his wife.
I have 15 or 20 such case histories. I do not need to read any more, other than to raise the questions which these social workers raise. They are questions that I think we, as legislators, should seek to answer. These are the questions raised by these social workers. What does a father of a family do, who is unemployed, not eligible for unemployment insurance, who day after day has gone out to look for work and day after day has had to come back at night without a nickel with which to buy food? How does he act with the most responsibility for his wife and children; by continuing to come home and thus ensure their continued hunger and possible eviction, or by desertion after which they will be taken care of by our municipal welfare departments? What health problems are we creating for the future? What does serious malnutrition over weeks and sometimes months do to adults and children? What about families whose only food for a week has been the stale loaves given to them by a sympathetic bread salesman who cannot bear to see them starve, and the mother giving a young baby sugar and water three days at a time, right in the city of Toronto? What is the use of all our research into the importance of nutrition, particularly during pregnancy, to mothers who cannot even be assured of a minimum diet?
Those are a few of the questions being raised by these social workers. Here is a government that has receded from the position of responsibility for providing employment when private industry fails, that has receded from the position of providing unemployment assistance apart from unemployment insurance, and that, finally, apparently makes no effort to bring under unemployment insurance those large groups who still remain outside, particularly the tens of thousands of young people who are seeking employment for the first time.
I suggest that the government should reconsider its whole stand and revert to the position it took in 1945. Those proposals were sound. Those proposals had the backing of every party in the house. Those proposals had the backing of the government's own research workers and economists. Those proposals are as sound today as they were in 1945. The fact that the government has not been able, in the course of ten years, to reach the agreements it desired with the provinces is no good reason why the government should shirk its responsibility regarding employment and the needs of those who are unemployed.

There is one thing the government can do to relieve a great deal of the distress existing at the present time and which will exist throughout the coming summer. It can extend the supplementary unemployment insurance benefits to the end of May at least, and make them retroactive to the date on which they were cancelled. That in itself will relieve some of those people who are now unemployed, cannot get employment and have no unemployment insurance benefits. I suggest that extension of the unemployment insurance benefits is the very least that a government having any concern for the problem of unemployment or the needs of the people who are unemployed should do at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise one point I have raised before but which, it seems to me, is worth repeating. I think one of the greatest weaknesses in the unemployment insurance set-up as it exists in Canada today lies in the fact that pregnant women are excluded from its benefits. I know that the most vexatious cases with which I have to deal are those arising out of the clause excluding pregnant women.
It seems to me that when the act was framed in the beginning there was some justification for this provision, but now that we have had 12 to 15 years' experience of the legislation in operation we have learned enough to establish that to include pregnant women in the benefits of unemployment insurance would not cause any undue drain on the finances of the country and would remove what I think is a great human grievance.
I do not want to get into the argument arising out of the statement made by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill), but I want to place it clearly on the record that I believe the most desirable way to increase the population of Canada is to increase it in the way the Almighty himself intended it to be increased when he said, "Be fruitful and multiply and replenish the earth."
Therefore when we come to the Unemployment Insurance Act I do not think it is a very good principle to be too technical about ruling out a woman who happens to be pregnant. Over the past few months I have had several women writing to me saying that after paying into the unemployment insurance fund for many years they became pregnant and were much astonished to find that they were excluded from the benefits. There is another point I want to raise, because I am not a member of the industrial relations committee. I certainly hope that the matter I have mentioned will be brought
Unemployment Insurance Act before that committee. I hope the whole question will be examined and evidence given by those able to do so as to what it would cost the country to make this necessary change.
If a thorough investigation of the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Act were really made-I am not talking now about the committee-I think we would find there are a great many abuses in the way benefits are drawn by certain people, and even certain abuses involved in the way that industry looks upon unemployment insurance. I am not at all sure that some industries do not look upon unemployment insurance as simply a means whereby they can keep on hand a certain number of reserve workers, to be laid off when they feel like laying them off. They know they will not disperse too quickly because of the unemployment insurance benefits; therefore they can bring them back when they feel like it.
I for one would not want to be too specific about abuses, but I am informed by people who should know that in a great many cases women who become pregnant manage to make themselves made eligible for unemployment insurance benefits by knowing what to do at the right time and by having the whole situation fixed up in the right way. In other words the woman who is absolutely honest, who has her baby in the right way, who walks up to the unemployment insurance office and says, "I am pregnant", is the one who is told that she is not entitled to any benefits, so she really gets it both coming and going. She has to undergo the expense of having the child; yet in spite of the fact that she needs money she is not entitled to any benefits whatsoever.
I for one believe this great country is rich enough and has had enough experience with unemployment insurance to remove what I consider to be an unnecessary, vexatious and most unjust discrimination against women who should be the deepest and most cherished concern of all the people of Canada, the working women of Canada who are adding to our population in the way the Almighty intended them to do.

Mr. Speaker, to begin with I should like to refer to the remarks of the last speaker. I suggest that probably he and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration should get together and bring their influence to bear upon the government, because there seems to be some question as to how the increase in the population of the land should be brought about. Possibly their combined influence would be of some help in solving this very vexatious problem.

Unemployment Insurance Act
In so far as criticism is concerned, I think perhaps I can go along with the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) when they say that the Minister of Labour is doing a remarkable job and should not have this government's errors of omission and commission chalked up against him. They said he was not to blame, that his department is concerned with unemployment and finding work for the unemployed, that is providing some form of subsistence within the framework of the Unemployment Insurance Act for those who are out of work.
Well, if he is not to blame, we must look elsewhere. This government have taken credit for everything that has happened in this country for the last 25 years; therefore we have to place on their doorstep the blame for the unemployment condition that exists in the country today. Whether or not we can tie the responsibility down to any particular minister is questionable, but I suppose in the aggregate they have to take responsibility for what the government does.
I should like to follow up the criticism offered by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) concerning the unemployment insurance bill that has been submitted to this house. It is contended this bill improves the act, but there is one weakness in that argument or at least it is not on very solid ground. The minister has said that there is going to be a change in the amount of benefit the unemployed can receive. For instance, in explanation of the move he said that those receiving benefits for from one to 19 weeks made up 90-1 per cent of the total. Those receiving benefits from 20 to 29 weeks comprise 6-4 per cent, and those receiving benefits for over 30 weeks comprise 3-5 per cent. The reason he gave for reducing the benefit period from 51 weeks to 30 weeks was that the average claim was for 9 weeks.
However, the supplementary benefits are to continue when the unemployed have exhausted the regular benefits they have built up. In other words, the total period during which benefits can be received will now be 45 weeks. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) mentioned certain abuses in connection with the operation of the fund. I believe this is an outstanding example of a place where abuses do not exist, according to the minister's own submission. It is quite apparent to everyone in the house that there has not been any abuse, and that the inherent honesty of these people is so great that they have not attempted to exhaust their benefits. They went back to work as soon as possible. This speaks very well for the people covered by the fund, and I feel that people who show


such outstanding honesty should not be subjected to any abridgment of their rights. The benefit provision should remain as it is because, as we all know, during the last two or three winters the period of unemployment has been gradually extended and the numbers of unemployed have been increasing. There is not much argument, therefore, for reducing the number of weeks for which benefits can be received.
If the government do pass this provision, they are working an injustice on the people by reducing the period of benefit from 51 to 30 weeks. The supplementary benefit period is 15 weeks, and when it is all added up it makes 45 weeks. Under the old scheme the unemployed received benefits for 51 weeks plus 15 weeks, but now that is to be reduced. Before reducing this period the government increased the amount that could be received both during the 51-week period and also during the supplementary benefit period.
_ This is a kind of double shuffle game. It is the old shell game; first you see it and then you don't. If the benefit period were left as it was and the payments increased, that would be worth while. The minister should be highly commended for the increase in the payment, but I think the government should be severely criticized for this double shuffle hocus-pocus that has been delivered to the unemployed.
Then there is the provision concerning those who retire at 65. These people have been paying into the fund but have never received benefits and were never expected to receive any benefits. They are compelled, under force of circumstances, to retire. It is' quite true that they are given a three-year reprieve; nevertheless they are deprived of something to which they are justly entitled. I think the minister would be well advised to reconsider that provision and bring it more into conformity with the principles of justice.
There is one other point that was mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton West concerning clause 3, paragraph 4. It reads as follows:
A commissioner may be removed by the governor in council at any time for cause, and a commissioner ceases to hold office upon attaining the age of 65 years.
I should like to put added emphasis upon that clause, for the simple reason that I have received suggestions on many occasions from labour department brochures that some means should be found of amplifying the opportunities for employment of those people who are unfortunate enough to have reached 65 and are going to lose their position. The suggestion has been that something should be done to broaden the field of employment for

these people. Here we find the government setting an example for everyone else to follow. I believe the members of this house have had the fact brought home to them rather forcibly upon learning that some of the stenographers who have served long and well are going to be retired at 65, whether or not they are giving good service. I think probably the government should search their souls on this question. I do not want to dwell on this point, but if the government are going to emphasize it in the general labour fields they should support it.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said the civil servants were supposed to have a guaranteed annual wage or a guaranteed job, yet we find they have not. Some of them have been let out. Some of those who have been let out were probably within two or three months of ten years' service, but they were put on the skids. They are being gradually let out, so the civil service does the very same thing of which business is accused, in that it lays off its employees. We see that most of these glaring examples have taken place in civil service groups, whether they are employed by provincial or federal governments. If it appears that the time is near when they will be classified as permanent employees, then on some pretext or other an excuse is found for letting them out before they qualify as permanent employees. And I have no doubt this government has resorted to that sort of practice. I suggest further consideration should have been given before this measure was brought in, with a view to giving work to older people.
Before passing on to another point, I would direct my remarks to the statement by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) that he would like anyone to point out any time in this country's history when an unemployment situation had been solved. He proceeded to say that his question could not be answered. Let me tell him that it can be answered.

This is a contributory insurance scheme. I say this provision is going to drive more people into the position where they will have to seek help from welfare agencies.
When the act was inaugurated we understood one of its purposes was to remove the necessity of appealing to the welfare agencies. Instead of removing that necessity, this

Unemployment Insurance Act measure aggravates the condition over a period of years. I suggest the period should be restored to 51 weeks, where it rightfully belongs. Instead of improving the situation we see today, I say it will be made worse under these amendments.
I sympathize with the larger cities, where the unemployment situation predominates, in their efforts to meet the problem. I do not intend to discuss the subjects set out in the green book of 1945, any more than to say that the government has gotten out from under its undertakings and promises of that time. If the government had carried out what it suggested in 1945 I doubt whether we would have this unemployment situation today, affecting those who are classified as the employable unemployed.
My chief criticism today is that an injustice is being done those people who have been paying into the fund for a long time. An injustice is being done those people who have been honest in their applications for assistance under the act. Not only that, but an injustice is being done in that these people, when their benefits expire, are being forced onto the relief rolls in the cities.
The federal government has made promises and recently abandoned them, and now the municipal and provincial governments find they have to assume this burden, one very much like that of the hungry thirties.
Some hon. members have referred to the guaranteed annual wage. I would go along with the hon. member who levelled criticism against the automobile industry. In my view the worst offenders who have been responsible for this condition of unemployment, or who have aggravated it in the past, have been those connected with the automobile industry. While they paid high wages and gave employment for certain limited periods of the year, their employees were laid off and thrown on the relief rolls for the balance of the year in the hungry thirties.
