Since the Unemployment Insurance Act became effective in 1941 many modifications have been brought about. One of these, made in 1950, applied to the logging and lumbering industry. Today I shall direct my remarks to that industry, as it exists in the constituency I have the honour to represent.
I hope my words will not be construed as a criticism of the department, because I take this opportunity to thank the minister and the government for the great care they took


at the time of the amendment in 1950, following representations not only from my district but from other parts of Canada. I would hope that what I say today would receive consideration when the bill is referred to the committee on industrial relations.
Under article 26 of the regulations the lumbering and logging industry of the province of Quebec is considered a seasonal industry. That is, it is an industry purporting to run from September 30 to April 1. This may have been true five or six years ago, at which time lumbering and logging in Quebec took place for the most part in the winter months. In the last two or three years conditions have changed to a very great extent. The result is that today lumbering and logging operations in the province of Quebec extend into the month of June. I know that right today in the constituency of Charlevoix lumbering is taking place on a scale just as great as in the months of December and January. This change has been brought about through the use of mechanical devices in the lumbering industry. A person who is now employed in lumbering sees his benefit curtailed as soon as the seasonal period ends, owing to this seasonal restriction; or if it is not curtailed he is required to possess more qualifications than the ordinary employee.
One has to understand how the lumbering business is carried on to appreciate the discrimination which exists against that group of employees under the law. In the province of Quebec a person goes into the woods lumbering early in September and carries on all winter long. In a few instances he leaves the job around the end of April, to come back again around May 15 to get the wood out. That is known as the hauling business in the industry. When that is finished around June 15 many of these employees, who are sons of farmers, find that they are out of jobs and they often go back to the farms to carry on during the summer months the same type of work they had been doing during the winter, with the exception that the farms usually belong to their fathers, or the farms are family units.
Under the law, people who work on farms cannot qualify for unemployment insurance. Therefore these people again suffer discrimination when they become unemployed the following year, because the period during which they were employed on the farm cannot be counted as a period that would entitle them to stamps. When the bill goes before the committee I hope consideration will be given to either extending the seasonal period for lumbering in Quebec or to treating lumbering and logging in the same

way they are treated in British Columbia, in the light of the change that has taken place in that particular industry in the last two or three years.
The law as it now stands discourages people in the logging industry from accepting employment with farmers who are also cutting wood for the pulp and paper industry. The farmer himself is experiencing some trouble because he finds it very hard to get people to work on his farm cutting wood. One can understand why people do not like to work for farmers. It is because they cannot take advantage of the Unemployment Insurance Act as it now exists. From the employer's point of view it is rather embarrassing, because he finds it very hard to get employees. The employee is reluctant to accept a job on a farm, and he would rather try, even if he loses time, to get a job in a place where he can get some unemployment insurance benefits after the work is done.
I also believe that from an administrative point of view it is a most complicated matter. I have examples, which have been submitted to me, of persons who have been employed in the lumbering industry from the month of October to the month of May. Then they went on a farm to carry on the same type of work. During the summer one of those persons applied for benefits from the unemployment insurance fund. Before he could get anywhere he received four letters, three in the same day, explaining why he could not qualify. The other letter explained why he did not have enough stamps. It was a request for a prolongation of time. I presume that meant that to establish his period of benefit he would have to go back two years and try to find some more stamps. The third letter explained that unless this time was obtained by him he could not benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act, because he had worked on a farm.
This qualification which is imposed on a person working either in the lumbering industry or on a farm is, I should say, very hard to understand, because in the province of Quebec, and especially in my riding, it very often happens that the man who goes on a farm cannot qualify although the farmer sometimes has only chickens and perhaps a couple of cows to look after. I do not think that should be called a farm, because this man has a small farm and derives most of his revenue from outside his farm.
It might be appropriate if in some parts of this country the word "farmer" were defined. If it is very hard to define the word "farmer", then part of this country should be divided into zones and the people in those zones should be called farmers or employees
Unemployment Insurance Act working in the lumbering and logging industries. That would avoid a lot of trouble in the administration of this act.
I do not make these comments to criticize the government. In the light of the changes which have been made in the lumbering industry everywhere in Canada, where mechanical devices have been introduced, such as huge tractors to clear away the snow and equipment to improve the roads so operations can be carried on from October 1 to May 31 or sometimes into June, I would urge the unemployment insurance commission to revise its regulations and make the employment unseasonal. If it has to be seasonal it should be from early September to the end of June.
If that were done, many employees whose main living is made in the bush will be able, when they are unemployed, to take full advantage of the law. They will not be placed in the position that some other qualification will be required of them to obtain benefits under the law. I make this plea because of the many representations I have received from farmers and people employed in the logging industry in my riding.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it must be obvious to the Minister of Labour from the speeches that are being made today that there are quite a few improvements that still have to be made in the Unemployment Insurance Act. Surely it is significant that suggestions as to shortcomings in the act are being made not only by members in opposition groups but also by those members of the Liberal party who thus far have participated in the debate today.
It seems to us, now we have had a chance to study the actual bill since the debate on April 4, at which time we had the resolution and first reading of the bill, that the main improvements in the bill are in the nature of administrative changes. Most of these changes are to the good. As has been pointed out, there are some which although administratively are an improvement are not too beneficial to the workers. However, our complaint is that although there have been many administrative changes there has not been enough change in the act in terms of policy and in terms of real substance.
As I pointed out when I spoke during the resolution stage on April 4, we feel that the action the government took in 1940, in asking parliament to concur in a resolution seeking an amendment to the British North America Act to write unemployment insurance into section 91 of that act, had the effect of obligating the government, morally if not

Unemployment Insurance Act legally, to federal concern over unemployment and federal responsibility for all unemployed. Government spokesmen may make different comments on the subject now, but we feel that the acceptance of that moral obligation arising from what was done in 1940 was confirmed by the green book proposals of 1945, when the federal government talked in terms of full federal responsibility for the employable unemployed.
Even we in the opposition could not complain too strenuously when the first Unemployment Insurance Act failed to go all the way in that direction, but surely when the time has come for an overhaul of the Unemployment Insurance Act the government should be making further progress in the direction of the moral obligation that was undertaken in 1940. In our view the government should now meet the commitment that we feel was made in this field by the government in 1945. However, we look in vain in this legislation for any broadening of the acceptance by the government of federal responsibility for all unemployed Canadians.
On the other hand, at the second reading stage on April 26, which was the same day the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made his speech to the federal-provincial conference in the railway committee room, we had the statement of the Minister of Labour that in certain circumstances he regarded what was proposed by the Prime Minister as more appropriate than unemployment insurance. I must be fair to him and say that he was speaking particularly of people along in years who at present are able to qualify under certain circumstances for 51 weeks of unemployment insurance benefits but who under the terms of this new bill will qualify for only 30 weeks of benefits unless they are able to qualify for supplementary benefits for a few weeks.
It does seem to us a shameful admission on the part of the government for the Minister of Labour to say that what was proposed by the Prime Minister, namely a form of relief-that is what it is, even though it is to be shared among three levels of government-was more appropriate in some cases than unemployment insurance benefits, which as we know have been built up in this country as something the workers have as a matter of right.
We feel that this is a retreat in principle; we feel that this is a retreat from the green book proposals of 1945; we feel that it is a retreat from the moral obligation which the federal government accepted when in 1940 it asked that insurance against unemployment be written into our constitution, into section 91 of the British North America Act.
Therefore, although the government and the unemployment insurance commission may have some feeling of satisfaction that when this bill is through the act will be in better form administratively than it was before, it is a disappointment to us that it does not move further in the direction of full federal responsibility for all employable unemployed.
When some others have talked in this vein the Minister of Labour has tried to suggest that this was an attack upon the actuarial soundness of the fund. The minister knows that some of the responsible labour bodies in this country have urged that those outside of unemployment insurance as we now have it should be covered by the federal government, but that the administration of whatever payments need to be made to these people should be under the unemployment insurance commission, with any additional grants of money that may be necessary to be made from the consolidated revenue fund. We feel that an approach of that kind would be much better than the one now being considered because it has been proposed by the Prime Minister. We feel that it would be more in line with the sound principles which the federal government laid before this country in the green books of 1945.
Because I spoke at some length on April 4, and because I expect to be a member of the committee to which this bill will be referred, I am not going to speak at length now. Neither am I going to raise all the issues which I feel we must raise when the bill is before that committee. However, there are one or two items which it seems to me are of sufficient importance that attention should be called to them now.
As I indicated in the reference I made a moment ago, I join with others in protesting against the reduction of the maximum period from 51 to 30 weeks. Here we have a case of the government giving with one hand but taking away with the other. I recognize that for three years after this bill comes into effect there will be no loss in actual dollars compared with what one would have had under the old act, but once that three-year period is over we will be down to the 30-week maximum rather than the 51-week. This will come at a time when the employment situation in Canada is still a question mark. We will be faced with all the various factors, including the tremendous factor of automation. We feel that this is no time to be reducing the maximum period for unemployment insurance benefits.
We feel that there is a deficiency in the new legislation in that although there are slight increases in the rates of benefit, the gap between the rates of benefit to be drawn
[Mr. ICuowtes.i

by insured workers and their wages before going on unemployment insurance is forever widening. The increase in benefits does not keep up with the increased cost of living, which is reflected in part in increased wages.
Workers who go on unemployment insurance today, or after this act goes through, even though they may get more dollars than was the case in 1940 or in 1945 will find the gap between what they are getting on unemployment insurance and what they were getting before they became unemployed much wider than it was. We feel that consideration should be given to the need of a higher rate of benefit.
I should also like to draw attention just in passing to a change which concerns me and which I have found in the section having to do with what we call the fair employment practices aspect of the Unemployment Insurance Act. As I read the section in the old act, which was put in only a few years ago, there was a small loophole in it. I admit that loophole was there, but it was a loophole of only two or three words. In the new act that loophole has been enlarged to two or three lines or even more. It seems to me that was a fairly important amendment, and I am sorry to see the loophole being made larger.
Likewise, Mr. Speaker, as an example of a type of change that is being made, may I say that I find the position of those employed by municipal public utilities is being altered. Under the old act the wording was such that employees of municipal public utilities were, by statute, made workers in insurable employment. Under the new act that is a matter of regulation; at least the commission can, by regulation, rule such employees to be excepted from the category known as insurable employment.
I mention that point, Mr. Speaker, because I am concerned about it in its own right, and also because I think it illustrates my point that in this legislation many changes have been made which seem to have as their aim the desire to make it a little easier to administer the legislation. I sympathize with the unemployment insurance commission in the tremendous job it has and the good job it does in administering this act, and I understand it wanting to have things so that they can be worked smoothly. We understand its desire to have leeway here and there so it can adjust things to fit various situations. But we do not like to see groups of people who were specifically covered put in an uncertain category, as is the case with those working for municipal public utilities.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to keep to my promise that I would save most of the points
Unemployment Insurance Act I want to raise on this bill until we get into committee. I am glad the minister has agreed that this bill is to go to the committee on industrial relations, where I know there will be representations from interested bodies and organizations. After we have been able to go over it in that committee I hope we shall be able to bring it back to the house a better piece of legislation than it is at the present time.
But even after we get such improvements as we can win in the Unemployment Insurance Act, I remind the government that this is not the whole answer to the tremendous problem of unemployment facing Canada at the present time.

I would appeal to the minister to extend this period beyond 30 weeks, for the following reasons. I think most Canadian workmen prefer to pay into the unemployment insurance fund and draw benefits while they are unemployed. They want to retain their selfrespect. They do not want to be obliged to depend on relief and charitable measures. If the unemployment insurance were paid for this full time, I think there would be less need for these relief measures. In these depressed areas I think it is fair to say that the people are less able than they otherwise would be to raise money for charitable purposes. Rents and taxes are in arrears. The people and the municipalities themselves are less able to raise money than when their economy is normal or buoyant.

Unemployment Insurance Act
We must not assume that a man who has not found work in the 30-week period does not want to find work. I know of a number of good, responsible men who have travelled across Ontario at least, getting rides with motorists, in an effort to find work. They have been unable to find work, and their benefits have expired. I was glad to see the seasonal benefits increased earlier this session. I am also glad to see the regular benefits increased under this act. However, I regret to see the time shortened with respect to payment of these regular benefits.
We live in a country of plenty, one with agricultural surpluses. I do not like to see anybody in this country go hungry because of our inability to deal with this particular phase of unemployment. I fully agree with the Prime Minister that we should not class those in need as employable and unemployable. The term "unemployable" is in many instances a relative one. Medical men are often puzzled to know how to classify these people. For example, a man might be unemployable as far as heavy, laborious work is concerned, but he might be better off physically and mentally if he had some lighter work to do.
In the debate at the resolution stage of this bill I emphasized the difficulties experienced by older workers in finding work, particularly the difficulty experienced by those 45 years of age or older in finding insurable employment under this act. Retirement at too early an age is causing a real social problem. In many cases it results in early physical and mental break-up. I have observed this result many times in my practice, and I am sure that is true in the case of other physicians. I would hope that our government will give consideration to this problem of the older worker, with a view to helping him prolong his years of contentment and usefulness.
I do not propose to deal with the other matters that I dealt with at the resolution stage of the bill. I then talked about wider coverage, but I think I shall leave that matter until the bill is in committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has shown realism and vision in bringing to this act such amendments as are likely to benefit the unemployed. Moreover, as evidenced by the proposals recently submitted to the provinces at the preliminary federal-provincial conference, the government clearly has no intention of shirking its responsibilities in connection with


unemployment and is resolved to implement whatever measures are necessary to solve this problem.
There is nothing surprising in the fact that this new bill respecting unemployment insurance is more generous and liberal, while imposing on the worker as small an increase as possible in those contributions necessary to give effect to this splendid social legislation. The minister has tried to make this legislation more flexible by requiring that contributions be now collected on a weekly rather than on a daily basis. The increase in benefits from $24 to $30 for married people and from $17.10 to $23 for single people will make it easier for these unemployed to provide for the basic necessities of life.
An important point to consider is that the integration of seasonal benefits, granted early this session, together with the advantages that will come out of this redraft, aimed at alleviating current unemployment, are not a result of a temporary measure merely for the duration of the present slack period. On the contrary, it will remain permanently in our statutes and, for years to come, citizens affected by seasonal unemployment will benefit from it.
I wish to commend the government for its energetic efforts to ease the people's burden and for its evident desire constantly to improve the lot of the workers.
Like everybody else in this house, I am eager to see this bill adopted, although I think it my duty to call the attention of the government to certain aspects of that legislation which have to do with men employed in lumber camps. In the province of Quebec, employment in the lumber trade and industry has been insurable since April 1, 1950. I might recall that, early in the first session of last parliament, I insisted on having lumberjacks covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act, because I felt that those who are most affected by the ups and downs of the employment situation are in the greatest need of protection.
The commission then thought that most workers in that industry only worked part of the year. That is why it was declared seasonal and a subsequent ruling imposed additional reservations with regard to the receipt of unemployment insurance benefits during the off-season. In the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, this off-season extends from April 1 to September 30.
Conditions in which lumbering operations take place tend to change from year to year. Automation, for instance, has contributed to

change the lumber industry into a year-round proposition.
Thus tractors and trucks are put to use as early as September and October and, very often, lumbering operations start just after the floating of the timber, usually between May 15 and July 15. The off-season for the lumberman therefore actually extends from July 15 to September 1st, while during the rest of the year he is actively engaged in cutting and other related operations. That is why I am requesting that seasonal regulations be lifted in the case of lumbermen. I am well aware that enforcement of these regulations is a source of misunderstanding, misapprehension and bother. By exempting the lumber industry from seasonal regulations, the commission would only generalize a situation which is already prevailing in the same industry in western Canada, especially in British Columbia.
I would not like to resume my seat without a word on behalf of the farmer who, during the slack season on the farm, goes out to lumber camps. Because of regulations governing seasonal employment, he does not qualify for unemployment insurance benefits unless he can prove that he has worked at least 135 days during the active farming season.
Mr. Speaker, those regulations are outmoded and complicate the life of everybody, including the insured people as well as the administration. I know that the intention of the government in making this revision is to apply the benefits of the act to more people, so as to extend the scope of this excellent social legislation. I am therefore satisfied that the commission, which is being authorized by the present act to draft regulations, will take my suggestions into account.
Mr. Speaker, I live in a district where lumbering operations are of prime importance. I know lumbermen very well and I know too of their needs and of their problems. That is why I am confident of speaking on their behalf when I request that they be exempted from the regulations regarding seasonal employment. The small farmer and the settler, who has to work away from home in the wintertime to earn a living for their family would undoubtedly be grateful if the commission decided to show more generosity towards them when drafting the new regulations, so that they may benefit, in the same proportion as other workers, from the unemployment insurance stamps they have in their books.

I believe you are quite right, Mr. Speaker. I was merely suggesting my reason

Then looking over Bill No. 328, which is now under consideration, I think perhaps the entire bill has been covered both at the resolution stage and now on second reading. The history of the Unemployment Insurance Act was reviewed. This is a complete revision of the act, 121 sections. It is divided into five parts, and I think we all give the minister credit for introducing this in a businesslike way.
There is one phase of the life of our people that has not been covered in this bill to the extent I believe it should have been. I feel that perhaps we are not aware of this group of people to the same extent we are aware of the entire labour and employment field. I was pleased to hear the previous speaker, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), refer to the older age group who are increasingly becoming a problem in our community life. There is a new interest in this age group. Those of us who represent industrial ridings and have calls for employment assistance, relief and other considerations, would probably all agree that people from 55 to 65, the non-veteran group, are a serious problem.
Recently the Canadian Welfare Council published a special issue dealing with this problem. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps this legislation could take more cognizance of this age group than has been the case. Some interesting facts in connection with this group are contained in this special issue, but I shall not go into them. The entire issue presents the case for this group, and I merely suggest that this legislation does not seem to be completely in conformity with the present plans of the department. The department published an interesting booklet concerning the problems of the older worker, and I have looked it over. It is probably fair to say that it does show an interest, but that interest was not carried through into this legislation.
I refer specifically to the controversial provision in this legislation which has been mentioned by nearly all the speakers so far, concerning the reduction of the maximum benefit period in the year from 51 to 30 weeks. It is true that less than 4 per cent of those receiving benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act during the year take the full 51 weeks now available. It is true that the transition period which has been planned for the next three years does assist this situation. It is true also that the seasonal benefits which were added this year do add 15 weeks of benefit in some cases, but I suggest this matter has not been covered completely in this reduced period.

I have some figures I should like to mention that are contained in the annual report on benefit years established and terminated under the Unemployment Insurance Act for the calendar year 1953. The source is the dominion bureau of statistics. Persons over 60 receive a relatively high proportion of the total benefit days paid. Such persons received 8,125,160 or 18-2 per cent out of a total of 44,660,188 benefit days paid on benefit years terminated during the calendar year 1953. While they received 18 -2 per cent of the total benefit days paid, persons over 60 accounted for only 10 per cent of the total benefit years terminated in 1953. I think it is fair to say that elderly people are apt to be eligible for the maximum duration of regular benefits. Retired persons who have paid into the fund for some time, therefore, constitute the group most largely affected by the reduction in the maximum benefit allowed from 51 to 30 weeks.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, while this legislation is welcome to some extent, this reduction is going to create a hardship on our older citizens, those who have been forced to retire at 60. In the past they were able to take the full 51 weeks' benefits, but now that is being cut down to 30 weeks, with a possible extension through supplementary benefits. I do-suggest there is a slight inconsistency in the attitude of the department toward this age group when they send out propaganda in connection with them, yet do not consider them to the fullest extent in this change that is being made.
No reason for the change was given by the minister, except that only a small percentage would be affected. I do hope that when the measure is before the committee every consideration will be given to the employment problem of this older age group, which is becoming such a sore spot in our community.

Mr. Speaker, when one rises at this stage of a debate he is apt to discover that not all of his thinking on the principle of a bill, such as the one we have been considering, has been completely unique or original. So perhaps I shall take as read some portions of the speech I had intended to make.
Nevertheless there are some matters which have not yet been touched upon by other

hon. members which I feel are of sufficient importance to merit consideration at this stage. I should like to mention those while I have the opportunity, and before this bill goes to the committee on industrial relations for consideration. May I say that, along with a good many other members, I am very happy that this type of study is to be given to the bill.
I think it becomes evident that one's reaction to the bill and the changes it proposes to make in our Unemployment Insurance Act depends very much upon the context in which one is considering it. One or two hon. members from this group who have preceded me in the debate have pointed out that the bill, and the general set-up of unemployment insurance, come far from meeting all the needs that arise in respect of unemployment and the problems connected therewith. I would suggest that those shortcomings arise largely from the fragmentary and piecemeal nature of the various measures of social security which thus far we have seen put into effect in Canada. However, if one does consider the bill in a narrower context, that is in relation to the present Unemployment Insurance Act, then I for one am inclined to feel that on balance this bill does represent something by way of a step forward in our unemployment insurance legislation. For that reason I am happy to see many of the provisions the bill proposes to introduce.
Along with others I have been giving special thought to those sections of the bill which have to do with the qualifying period, and the changes made in respect of the duration of the benefits. I think we must recognize that while this bill applies to a broad group of Canadian citizens, nevertheless under the present act, and even if the bill now proposed becomes law, the fact still remains that those able to secure benefits under the unemployment insurance legislation will remain in effect a privileged group of Canadian citizens.
It can be argued that under certain circumstances the clause in the bill which changes the qualifying arrangement from that of so many contribution days to that of so many contribution weeks does make it somewhat easier for persons to achieve qualification under the bill. Nevertheless it still remains a long way from providing that principle of complete insurance coverage which I suggested in a former speech could very well be applied and must be applied before this legislation is all that it should be. I suggested that, following through with the generally accepted insurance principle, it should be possible if one had paid, in effect, one premium under unemployment insurance,
Unemployment Insurance Act such person should thereby become qualified to benefits if, through no fault of his own, the need for such benefits became apparent.
I still feel that should be our objective.
Obviously the present measure falls far short of measuring up to that kind of requirement. I do appreciate that section of the bill which increases the minimum period of benefits, the period during which people who have not achieved a great length of contribution under the bill can receive benefits, if they become qualified. To my way of thinking that does go some distance toward meeting the needs of those who are most likely to require the benefits.
There has been a great deal of talk over the fact that the maximum period for which benefits can be paid is being reduced from 51 to 30 weeks, and I know that various labour groups in the country have been making representation on this point. So long as the general situation in Canada continues in its present state, representations are going to continue to be made on that point. However, it has become apparent to me that the approach the government has taken toward the question of unemployment insurance coverage is still basically that outlined some time ago by the minister, when he said it was designed to meet the needs of frictional and seasonal unemployment. I suppose it might be argued that under the Unemployment Insurance Act as we have understood it thus far in Canada, that is all this particular legislation is designed to do. This particular proposal in the bill makes it clearer than ever that that is still in the mind of the Minister of Labour and in the minds of his colleagues in proposing the present measure.
I might point out that the fact this proposal is being advanced makes it more evident than ever to me that there is a need in the country for something over and above what we have in our Unemployment Insurance Act. It may be true, as the minister has pointed out, that the proposal contained in the bill will meet the needs of those requiring unemployment insurance benefits or at least a large percentage of them. However, that still does not alter the fact that there are people in the country who are going to need something more than that; and when one hears talk about developing automation, and when one gets little glimpses every so often of the speed with which technological change is taking place in the country, then, should the bill return to the house for third reading with the proposal for a 30-week maximum intact, it will become more apparent than ever that we do need to have

I am glad to see that provision is made in the bill for a three-year period during which the present arrangements can be tapered off. I should like to suggest that in that three-year interval the government might give serious consideration to the proposals advanced in the form of the resolution I had on the order paper last session and again this session, having to do with a new national insurance plan covering individuals against dislocations caused by technological advances, changed marketing conditions and other related causes. If we can have some serious indication from the government that they have some such proposal in mind in order to deal with those other problems related to the unemployment question which, it has been made plain by the statement of the minister, the present Unemployment Insurance Act is not designed to cover, then there would be a good deal less concern over this proposal to reduce the maximum period during which benefits can be paid.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite willing to bow to your ruling in that regard. It was not my intention to go into a detailed analysis of the section. It was merely for convenience of reference that I mentioned the number. I hope Your Honour will agree that in a bill of this kind complex principles are involved.
I wish to discuss the matter of excepted employment. Reference has already been made in the debate to one particular aspect of the subject, namely the fact that employment


in the fishing industry is still excepted employment. I am very glad to know that a number of hon. members have taken up this matter. The present bill still proposes to except those who are employed in the great fishing industry of this country from the coverage of unemployment insurance. This is a matter on which I feel very strongly myself. It is a fairly complex matter.
I should like to have some assurance from the minister that when this bill goes to the committee thorough consideration will be given to all aspects of that matter so hon. members can discuss in detail the pros and cons that it is not possible for us to discuss at this stage of the debate. I hope following that discussion the bill will come back to the house with an arrangement whereby those in the fishing industry will come within the provisions of the bill as we finally pass it.
One other group of people are mentioned as being in excepted employment, and I should also like to refer to them. It is a fact that those employed in a hospital not operated for purposes of gain are still listed among those in excepted employment. Unless my understanding of the situation throughout this country is completely wrong, the proportion of hospital beds involved in institutions which are operated for gain is very small indeed in Canada. Therefore, for all practical purposes the section eliminates from the coverage of the bill those who are employed in hospitals.
I notice that provision is made for the commission, with the consent of the employer, to include those who are employed in hospitals that are not operated for purposes of gain. That principle is embodied in this bill. I feel that the sections which deal with it are completely at variance with the basic principle embodied in the bill. I suggest this section should be taken out of the bill. The fact that this bill makes the employees of the hospitals of this country subject to the whims and fancies of the employers is most repugnant to me. What does this mean? It means, for example, that a stationary engineer working in a sawmill or in a factory is in insurable employment, but if he moves into a hospital he disqualifies himself for the benefits of unemployment insurance coverage.
I might point out that another principle is expressly set out in the bill. It says that in determining whether any employment is or was insurable, regard shall be had to the nature of the work rather than to the business of the employer.
I understand that representations have been made on this question by those who are managing hospital institutions. If such representations have been made, I would suggest

that they represent a very serious blind spot in the thinking of those who may otherwise be carrying on a most useful and desirable function in the life of this country. I would suggest to them that the time has come, if they still hold those views, for them to revise their opinions.
Because of the way in which some hospitals and charitable institutions are run in this country, it may not be possible or desirable to have complete and universal coverage in that connection; but I would suggest that if that is the case this section could be much more desirably drafted by having it read in this way:	"At the request of the
employees, the commission shall bring these people into insurable employment".
In the province from which I come the hospitals are supported by the populace as a whole. It is a very poor situation when many thousands of workers who are supporting the hospitals are themselves covered by unemployment insurance, yet their fellow workers, who may be called upon to minister to them in their illness, because of some whim of the hospital board, are denied what to those who are patients is a right and privilege which they enjoy as Canadian citizens because of this act.
There is one other group of citizens of this country which is in effect an excepted group, although they are not named as such in the Unemployment Insurance Act. During my visit last year to Newfoundland I was surprised and shocked to learn that many hundreds and probably over the course of time many thousands of my fellow Canadian citizens in that province receive no benefits whatever under the Unemployment Insurance Act because they are or have been employed on certain leased bases in that province. I became interested enough in the situation to do a little reading on the subject to find out how it came about. I realize, as all members of the house do, that basically it arose out of a treaty to which Canada was not a party in the first place. I discovered that this treaty has been modified since the time Newfoundland became a part of Canada, and I assume there is a possibility that some further modifications might be made in that respect.
Apparently such modifications as have been made have not been such as would cover those who are employed, for example, by a civilian United States contractor at a leased base. As far as I can see that is not a good situation, that is not something which Canada as a whole should continue to countenance. I notice that article 28 of the original treaty makes provision for giving sympathetic consideration to any representations which either
Unemployment Insurance Act party to the agreement may make from time to time after the agreement has been in force. I notice also that after Newfoundland became part of Canada certain modifications were made.
On page 46 of treaty series 1952, No. 14, it is pointed out that arrangements were made whereby exemption from Canadian income tax, which apparently had been in effect, was removed from United States contractors or contractors ordinarily resident in the United States in respect of profits arising from work performed at the leased bases. I suggest that when such modifications of the treaty were made it would have been desirable at the same time that a further modification be made to require such contractors to have their employees covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act. However, I understand that was not done and, as I say, over the years many thousands of the citizens of Newfoundland have been denied the right to build up unemployment insurance coverage.
Unless the Minister of Labour can persuade the Secretary of State for External Affairs to make some immediate adjustment in the arrangements with the authorities of the United States of America, I would suggest that when this Unemployment Insurance Act is being revised provision should be made to cover these people. Those of us who live in the rest of Canada and who directly or indirectly were responsible for the partial alienation of what is now Canadian soil should be prepared to accept the responsibility of seeing that no citizen of Newfoundland is thereby deprived of his right to unemployment insurance. If it is necessary to draft an arrangement whereby the unemployment insurance commission will assume the employer's share in connection with workmen engaged in these areas, I think that is something this parliament could very well support.
I realize that there are a number of matters in respect to this bill which have not been touched upon either by myself or by other hon. members. There may be other hon. members who wish to take part in the debate, and certainly there will be opportunity for full discussion of all sections of the bill when it gets into committee. Therefore I shall not prolong my remarks at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for York South have as usual offered the constructive criticisms and suggestions which are put forward by this party and other members of our group. There is no necessity for me to

Unemployment Insurance Act take up the time of the house to repeat them, but I do want to bring to the attention of the house and the minister two or three groups who are excluded under the present bill whom many of my constituents would like to see included.
Before proceeding with this matter, I must say that I was most interested in listening to the debate this afternoon to note the exceptionally large percentage of Liberal members who spoke in the debate who had criticisms to make of the bill and suggestions to offer to the minister. I was most interested in listening to the two hon. members from the province of Quebec who spoke just prior to the recess at six o'clock, and I noticed that both hon. members put forward criticisms very similar to those I am going to make at this time.
First of all I refer particularly to farm workers. A good many of the people I represent are very sorry that farm workers are not included in the coverage of this legislation. Farm workers should be covered by the act. In my opinion the present exclusion of farm workers is unfair to the farm worker and to the farmer.
I say it is unfair to the farm worker because it penalizes him for doing a most essential job, a job which is not popular with a great number of people in this country at this time. We should do everything possible to keep our farmers on the land and encourage farm workers to assist in the working of those farms. A farm worker usually works for lower wages and in many cases he has less security than the industrial worker. If any section of workers needs it, he needs this protection. I think we should do all we can by amending this legislation and in other ways to make employment on the farms of this country as attractive as possible.
I say it is unfair to the farmer because it makes it very difficult under some circumstances for him to obtain farm labour at the right time, particularly casual labour. I know that in my own constituency quite frequently a man would like to go to work on a farm for a month or two, but if he has any choice of employment at all he will accept employment where he is covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act. I think it is most unfair to the farmer as well as to the farm worker, because it puts the farmer in a difficult position when it comes to competing for necessary labour, particularly at certain periods of the year.
This is an extremely important matter to the farmers in my constituency, particularly those engaged in the fruit industry who usually do their pruning in the spring months of the year while the snow is on the ground,
[Mr. Herridge.I
then have considerable thinning to do in the summer months-ihere is a great deal of hand labour in orchard work-and then in the fall require extra help in the harvesting and packing of the fruit. It affects fruit farmers particularly, and other farmers as well. I say that the exclusion of farm workers from the terms of this act is unfair to the farm worker himself-it is distinctly unfair to him-and presents an unnecessary problem to the farmer.
Of such great concern is this matter to the farmers in British Columbia that I know it has been discussed at numerous farmers' conventions and farmers' institutes. I have heard it discussed at institute meetings in the Kootenay district and in other districts in British Columbia. It was the subject of considerable discussion at the recent convention of the British Columbia fruit growers' association held in Kelowna on January 18, 19 and 20. I might say that this is a convention of all tree fruit growers in the province of British Columbia covering the Okanagan, the Koote-nays and the main-line points along to the west of Kamloops.
This subject was of such great importance that it was raised on the first day of the convention, and considerable discussion took place. Then it was decided that it would be a good idea to get the head of the unemployment insurance office to come and address the convention, to inform the convention of the terms of the act and so on. This gentleman kindly came to the convention and gave an informative address to the delegates. Following his address there was a thorough discussion of the whole problem and by unanimous vote the delegates to the British Columbia fruit growers' association convention adopted this resolution:
Whereas in almost every other industry there are unemployment insurance benefits.
Therefore be it resolved by this 1955 British Columbia fruit growers' association convention that steps be taken through the proper channels to persuade the dominion government to include full-time farm workers in the national unemployment scheme.
I support that resolution, Mr. Speaker. I might say that I am one of those who have been asked to try to persuade the government to give effect to that resolution.
In addition to provision for full-time farm workers, I think provision should be made for part-time or casual farm workers. In our district we find a situation which is similar to that described by the Liberal member from Quebec who spoke prior to the recess at six o'clock. There are a great many farmers who carry on a combination of farming and lumbering. We have lumbermen who are willing to put in a few weeks on a farm, or

who would be willing to put in a few weeks on a farm if they could continue to be cover-ered by unemployment insurance benefits and so on.
I urge the minister to give serious consideration to these representations from the British Columbia fruit growers' association and other organizations, and to the requests that have been made in the house by members of the various parties during this debate. I also hope the committee will inquire thoroughly into this aspect of the question, because I am distinctly of the opinion that the exclusion of farm workers is unfair to those working on farms and is distinctly unfair to the farmers.
I now want to deal very briefly with another group. On April 4, when the resolution preceding this bill was under discussion, I raised this matter but, after listening to the minister and after carefully reading the record, I note that the minister did not rise to my bait. I am therefore now going to cast another fly in his direction. I want again to bring to the attention of the minister the unfairness suffered by certain groups, particularly in British Columbia. I refer to certain people who are employed in the forest branch to carry on tree planting, snag felling, land clearing and the burning of brush in order to provide forest protection and conservation. Here is what to me is a peculiar thing.
By an arrangement between the federal government and our provincial government the clerical staff, the research workers, the draftsmen, the mechanics, the scalers and the truckers of the British Columbia forest service receive unemployment insurance benefits, but the very men of whom I have spoken are not covered. These men are usually employed in the months of the year when there is no snow on the ground, and quite frequently they are laid off as soon as the first snow comes. At that time of year it is often extremely difficult for them to obtain employment. These men who work in the forest branch on forest conservation are the very ones who should be brought under the terms of this act.
I hope the minister gives consideration to that aspect of the problem, and I also hope the committee will study the question. I cannot understand the logic of the present arrangement. These men are doing almost exactly the same type of work as are the lumbermen in the woods, those working in the sawmills and for the logging companies. For instance, I was in a camp last summer in which men doing this work were not covered by the act. But the truck driver in the camp was covered, and the cook in the camp was covered. It is a situation that
9. 1955	3593
Unemployment Insurance Act creates some unfairness to these men who are willing to go in the woods in the summer and do this forest protection work. I ask that their case be given consideration by the minister and by the committee.
Before concluding, I want to support all those hon. members who have presented the case of the fishermen. I understood the minister to say that the matter was under study and was receiving careful consideration. I am not well acquainted with all the complexities of that occupation, but judging from the representations that have been made to members of this house and the representations that have been made by members of this house from all parties to the minister, I am quite confident that there must be a great deal of validity in the arguments put forward.
I trust that the position of farm workers, those engaged in the forest service of British Columbia in the conservation of our forests, and those employed in the fishing industry will receive from the minister, from the committee, and finally from this house the consideration that their situation and their contribution to our production deserves.

speechtext:
Before the minister closes the debate, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the reference by the hon. member for Kootenay West to casting a fly and hoping to catch a fish prompted me to make one more appeal on behalf of the fishermen.
It will be recalled that the Minister of Labour earlier this session said he was giving consideration to the finding of means by which the fishermen, and those to whom he referred as near-fishermen, might be included in the coverage under amendments which he hoped to bring in to this legislation.
I do not intend to repeat at any length the arguments I have advanced on behalf of these men who are employees of companies engaged in the fishing industry. In certain companies there are men employed in various trades. In these trades employees of other companies which are not actually engaged in fishing are covered. I have called the attention of the minister to the fact that it is necessary to maintain the fish traps and weirs. The number of piles to be driven at certain seasons of the year requires the fishing companies to employ pile drivers who work for companies which are engaged in the construction industry. Those pile drivers, working on the same project alongside the pile drivers who are employees of the fishing company, are covered by unemployment insurance, but those who are employees of the fishing company are not. I have referred to pile drivers, but there are several other

Unemployment Insurance Act kindred trades in which men are employed by the various companies engaged in the fishing industry.
Of course there is the question of the men who actually go out in the boats to harvest the fish from the ocean. A few of them own their own boats, but the majority are either working in some co-operative or are working as employees of a fishing company. Sometimes the query is raised as to who is going to pay the employer's contribution. I do not know whether the minister has explored the angle that the buyer of the fish, who is really the employer of the fishermen, might possibly be expected to pay the employer's contribution. These companies are keenly interested in the catch made by the fisherman. The success of the packing company or the purchasing company depends entirely upon his catch. Could they not be classed as the employers?
I have put the various arguments before the minister personally and in the house on other occasions. I am not going to repeat them, but I hope that when the bill goes to the committee some way will be found whereby employees of fishing companies and the fishermen themselves can be covered by unemployment insurance. I know the work of the fishermen is largely seasonal, but because they are engaging in more and more different types of fishing and are not restricting their catch to one particular species the work is being spread over a much longer period than was the case a few years ago. The work is not nearly as seasonal as it was 10, 15 or 20 years ago, and the fishermen must have different types of equipment to catch the various species of fish throughout the greater portion of the year in order that they may make a living.
I make a final appeal to the minister to urge the committee to which the bill is being sent to give the most earnest consideration to some way of covering the fishermen employed in this great industry on the Atlantic, the great lakes and the Pacific coast with unemployment insurance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the debate today has indicated the keen interest there is in unemployment insurance and in this measure to improve our Unemployment Insurance Act. I believe it is correct to assume from what we have heard this afternoon and this evening that nearly all the things we are trying to do in this measure meet with general approval. Of course there are strong
[Mr. Pearkes.l

differences of opinion as to how we should go about it, and as to some of the details.
I have made a note of the various points that have been raised in the different speeches. I noticed during this debate on second reading, when the principle of the bill is before the house or, as one hon. member said, the various principles of the bill, that most hon. members expressed the view that a closer examination should wait until the measure comes before the standing committee on industrial relations.
I think it would be well for me to follow that good example. In doing so, however, may I say that I appreciate the helpful and interesting manner in which the discussion has been carried on today. Even though I may not now dwell on the various points raised, I should like to assure hon. members that I am fully aware of their seriousness, and I give them the assurance that there will be a full opportunity for their discussion in the standing committee. For instance, just a few moments ago reference was made to fishermen. They and farm workers were mentioned this afternoon by a number of hon. members. I can tell the house that these matters have received and will continue to receive attention and study to see what we can do.
In saying that, I should like to state that the fringe group, if I may call it that, associated with the fishing trade, referred to by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, and the forestry group referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West, do not come exactly within the category to which I am referring now. I think we should have less difficulty in finding a formula for those two small groups than in the case of the main bodies of fishermen and farm workers.
I think the house will understand some of the difficulties that will face the committee when I say it is recognized, according to the 1951 census, that there were 50,222 non-wage earners amongst our fishermen, or 93 per cent, and 3,775 wage earners, or 7 per cent. I am not going to pursue that matter now; we shall discuss it again in the committee.
I can say with regard to these two groups that the commission can by regulation, subject to the approval of the governor in council, bring under the act any group of workers, and the commission constantly has in mind the possibility of increasing the coverage and bringing in as many people as possible. But there are a great many more difficulties, some of which have been referred to today, and they can be discussed when the bill goes to the committee.
Among other things, in the debate there was reference to seasonal benefits, the

length of the benefit period-perhaps talked about more than any other point-and the question of a closer relationship between the benefits and the coverage, which is a feature of the bill. In the first instance all these matters gave the commission and the government a great deal of concern before the measure was introduced. I feel the discussion today has been useful, and hon. members will be able to appreciate some of the other considerations when the bill goes to the committee.
