speechtext:
With all of it. I want to join with my colleagues and express my approval of the main motion now before us.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his masterful presentation of his first budget on April 5 last. The first annual statement of our finance minister has
50433-227i
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud been well received and favourably commented upon by the large majority of thinking Canadians. His belief that a healthy expansion of the Canadian economy is everybody's business will lead to greater activity in our entire national economy. He has taken a courageous position in providing a measure of tax relief to be enjoyed by personal income taxpayers and by corporations alike.
Some members of the opposition have criticized the minister and the government for budgeting for a possible deficit, while others have claimed that his deficit is far too small. The general feeling throughout the nation is that the attitude taken is sound, based on good judgment, and according to the principles of good business.
I also want to express my appreciation to the Minister of Finance for having included in this year's budget a clarification of two special items under schedule A of the Customs Tariff, which will be of immeasurable value to one of the leading manufacturers of my constituency and to the entire community.
Since the early part of 1953 base metal discoveries, followed by preliminary and normal development in the northern part of New Brunswick and particularly my constituency of Gloucester, have made news highlights. The great variety of minerals located in the Bathurst area, lending themselves in many cases to open pit mining, together with extremely low transportation costs, have led to the conclusion that New Brunswick could in the near future become one of the world's leading producers of lead and zinc. These discoveries were followed by substantial finds by American Metals Properties in the adjoining Miramichi area. Today prospects are bright for a mining future that could eventually revolutionize the entire economy of the maritime provinces.
It is recognized, however, that no mining developments of consequence and of advantage can expand without the availability of cheap electric power. No one can deny that cheap power is the key to New Brunswick's future mining development. I agree with previous statements to that effect made in this house by members from New Brunswick, whether originating from the opposition side or from the government side of this house. On different occasions the New Brunswick representatives on the government side of this house have been accused of not supporting the demand for federal assistance in the financing of hydroelectric projects for the province of New Brunswick. We realize that our mineral deposits must be developed in such a way as to be of maximum benefit to

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud ment in Canada, Outlook 1955, Regional Estimates". I want to quote from his remarks as reported at page 3231 of Hansard:
I followed along by saying that in New Brunswick things are beginning to move. We definitely have a good optimistic mood down there now. We have a new government. They have tackled our economic problems in a sensible way. We have invested in ourselves, Mr. Speaker. That is something which a great many of the other areas of Canada cannot say. We have led in that investment in ourselves in the last few years, and I put the figures on the record for everyone to see.
The figures which were placed on the record by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert showed that in 1953 New Brunswick had an industrial expansion of 7-9 per cent, and in 1954 it again led the way with an expansion of 27-7 per cent. What the hon. member failed to prove in the course of his remarks was who is responsible for this large increase in the capital expenditures made in the province of New Brunswick in the last two years.
To answer my hon. friend I shall quote' from the annual report of the province of New Brunswick, department of industry and development, 1954, as tabled in the provincial house during the last session of the New Brunswick legislative assembly by Hon. R. J. Pichette, minister of industry and development of New Brunswick. I shall then answer my hon. friend by quoting from a report originating with a provincial government which he is supporting, as are the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery). I quote:
While industrial development in the province this year did not reach the tempo we had expected, it is quite evident that the impetus to our economy being provided by Camp Gagetown and the sustained program of mineral exploration, spreading to almost all sections of the province is beginning to attract the favourable attention of a wide range of manufacturers, and services firms. Unquestionably, as camp Gagetown reaches full operational status and mining reaches the producing stage, we can expect industrial growth to keep pace.
Camp Gagetown, a federal project, and the mines financed by private enterprise are then responsible for this increase in capital expenditures in New Brunswick about which my hon. friend feels so proud. One must not neglect the importance to New Brunswick's economy of the construction of Camp Gagetown. While contracts amounting to $30 million have been awarded by Defence Construction Limited, as at February 1 of this year, it is estimated that further tenders amounting to $20 million will be let on this project within the next 12 months. This does not include the construction of 1,400 houses at a cost of approximately $16 million by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a project which will be undertaken in the near future.
One must not forget that the 10,000 servicemen training at this army camp and a permanent staff of 1,500 to 2,000 will add substantially to the general economy of the province of New Brunswick. I hold in my hand a bill to incorporate the town of Oromocto; a small village, previously unknown, will become a town owing to the federal project at Camp Gagetown. Already tenders are being called for the supply of perishable food, such as large quantities of bread, milk, and meat which will be used during the long training periods at this army camp, the largest in Canada.
When a decision has to be made on the construction of a central heating plant, there again consideration was given to New Brunswick and a central furnace will be installed which will use from 40,000 to 50,000 tons of Minto coal a year. In view of the numerous challenges which we have received in this house from opposition members, I feel it is my duty to place on the record figures which will tell the truth about the situation so far as New Brunswick is concerned.
Let me outline some of the federal expenditures for New Brunswick during the fiscal year 1955-56: Department of National Defence at Camp Gagetown, $50 million; at Chatham air base and Ste. Marguerite, $7 million; Department of Public Works, $16 million; Department of National Health and Welfare in hospital construction grants, $976,000; other health grants, $1,287,000; old age security, $12,600,000; old age assistance, $1,250,000; Blind Persons Act, $265,000; family allowances, $15 million, or a total of $104,378,000.
In other words, three of the federal departments will spend in New Brunswick this year over $100 million, which is over twice the total amount of the provincial budget for the same period. Furthermore, out of a total budget of $54 million the province of New Brunswick will receive in 1955 over $17 million from the federal government under the 1947 tax agreement, which is close to one-third of its total proposed expenditure. These are the figures, Mr. Speaker, that I want to place on record in answer to the challenge from the hon. members of the opposition.
I welcome the announcement by the Minister of Finance of the appointment of a royal commission with instructions to look ahead and examine carefully our future economic prospects. The maritimes are today placing their hopes in the field of mineral development. It has been recognized that to make the most of it, these minerals should be refined on the spot, and the erection of a smelter should be followed by the necessary plant for the production of acids and fertilizer from the

large sulphur content of its ores. The achievement of these objectives is only possible, as I have just said, by the introduction of a missing element, namely cheap electric power.
The first duty of this royal commission should be to launch without delay a complete study of the maritimes' general economy and its possibilities. It appears to be an established and well-recognized factor that the maritime provinces, and particularly New Brunswick, are not in a position to finance adequate power projects to permit the normal expansion of potential developments which could revolutionize the entire economy of this particular section of our great country. We cannot expect to solve our problems overnight; but we, as representatives of the Canadian people, have assumed a responsibility which none of us can deny. It is our duty to unite our efforts and assure the participation of the maritimes in the Canadian boom which to an astonishing degree is still confined to the industrial areas of central Canada.
These are my concluding remarks in the budget debate, Mr. Speaker, but before resuming my seat I want to assure hon. members of the opposition from New Brunswick, that I, as a sitting member on the government side, am in favour of any assistance and any government measure that will add to our provincial economy and to the welfare of our people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of entering this debate, but after listening to so much of the unadulterated buncombe about the government's record I just could not resist saying something about it. The taxpayer has found out to his sorrow that it is just pure illusion. The St. Laurent, Abbott and Harris dollar which they are receiving is worth less than 50 cents after all taxes are paid. The administration, because of its waste and extravagance, has had to levy higher taxes than are absolutely necessary.
One of the previous speakers, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), was quite strong in his adulation of the cabinet and the ministers of the crown. I did not know whether he was going to start out with a series of Studerisms, but I soon found out they were just plain ordinary "Studer-men", not supermen.
The government by its waste and extravagance has in devious ways punished every Canadian citizen who has been patriotic or prudent enough to invest in government bonds, or whose life savings are tied up in insurance or other forms of security. These people now realize what this government has done to them through its inflationary
The Budget-Mr. Small policies. Veterans and pensioners are likewise in the same position, because they are on fixed incomes. The rapid inflation has affected them also and reduced them to a subsistence allowance; it has almost impoverished them.
While the government is very glib in taking credit for all the social legislation enacted, the truth of the matter is that most of our welfare laws originated in the fertile minds of Conservatives, although this emaciated and decrepit form of Liberalism has leeched on to them and they have fattened, as they always have done on their exploitation of the ingenuity of others.
It might be advantageous to read an article by Bruce Hutchison published last week in which he outlined the progress made in Canada since confederation. He said that the only outstanding idea that had been developed in this country was confederation itself, and that was the brainchild of Sir John A. Macdonald. The next was Sir John's national policy, that has been the base of our prosperity. The next along the line was reciprocity, which the people of this country turned down in a very decisive manner. In as much as this government has by indirect methods tried to introduce reciprocity with the United States, they should have the courage to go to the people and tell them they are trying to inflict reciprocity on them again.
However, that is up to them and their conscience, if they have one.
Our standard of living has advanced, in spite of this government, because of the initiative and incentive of our people. They are the ones who have created the wealth of this country. Our wealth has been created through labour's continuous productivity, and it is not the invention of Mackenzie King, Louis St. Laurent or even the wizardry of Ilsley, Abbott or Harris. They were just the factual, physical substance that was carried forward on the strong flow of the nation's destiny, and if we have prospered it has been in spite of them.
Last year when the minister of finance presented his budget he was most nonchalant, free and easy and indulged in many loose conjectures, or what you might ordinarily call economic double talk, the gist of which was that we were going to have a good year if we did not run into the hard times that he saw ahead and hoped we would miss.
He forecast a surplus of $4 million, with a possible deficit of $140 million if the tough times he saw ahead arrived. Well we did have the tough going to the tune of a $160 million deficit.

The Budget-Mr. Small
There was considerable similarity between the budget of last year and the budget of this year, but they could not be called twins by any stretch of the imagination. This year the nonchalant manner of the previous minister of finance was lacking. Because it was his initial appearance the Minister of Finance this year was rather tense and nervous, which we all rather expected, but he did not abandon the same chopstick logic in the juggling of finance practised by his predecessor.
Last year the minister of finance played up the recommendations of the Randall commission in the United States, which were rejected, or which if accepted were ignored and not enforced. Here is what the Minister of Finance said last year, as reported at page 3724 of Hansard of April 6, 1954:
For most of this period the United States has been in the process of re-examining its foreign economic policies.
And again:
The recommendations of this commission-better known as the Randall report-provide, in my view, a reasonably promising basis for action by the United States in a co-operative movement towards a sounder system of trade and payments.
And further down:
-and it was recognized that enlightened economic policies on the part of both the United States and Canada would contribute materially to the achievement of a better trade and payments system throughout the free world.
And again:
To this end the United States administration has just placed before congress a program designed to give effect to the main recommendations of the Randall commission.
And finally:
As might be expected, this development has brought with it growing protectionist pressures in many countries, including Canada.
Here is what the present Minister of Finance said this year, as reported on page 2727 of Hansard of April 5:
In the past twelve months, however, while there was no basic change in American policies, there was a disappointing lack of progress toward actual reductions in trade barriers and there were disconcerting signs of a revival of protectionist feeling in response to the increase in competitive conditions.
I should remind the house that the United States administration has resisted proposals which, in our opinion, would not advance the cause of friendly and mutually advantageous trade. This resistance we welcome. On the other hand, it must be confessed that the resistance has not been uniformly successful. We all have our difficulties and it is not always possible to achieve ideal solutions. But it must be recognized that actions taken or even implied by the government of the United States may weaken support for liberal commercial policies and may impose upon those of us who are firm supporters of such policies a greater burden in defending them in our own countries.

And later:
It is of the utmost importance for the future of international economic co-operation that the United States should continue to give positive direction and leadership in reducing barriers to the free flow of world trade.
I could go on and quote more of this, but I think I have quoted sufficient to show that while efforts can be made to bring discord and frustration and impotence into an acceptable medley, acceptable to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the minister of external affairs, they have simply ended up in a muddle. They are very sorry for what has taken place, and they have expressed their outstanding and emphatic dissatisfaction with the policies of the United States.
Nevertheless they say we cannot do anything about it, because if we do they might slap us down. Therefore we must remain on good terms with them. This effort to reconcile the glaring barriers of United States protective policy with the intangible devices of the free trade policy of this government gives you the picture I have just outlined; it is too bad, but we cannot do anything about it.
This year there is such a hullabaloo made about the few changes in the budget that you really would think it was something. The budget contains a very few changes. The benefits certainly are lean, and they will not bring the kind of relief the taxpayers have been looking for. They have been looking for an increase in their exemptions and a considerable reduction in the hidden sales taxes of this country. Changes of this kind would have made an immediate and, I would say, effective improvement in the financial position of the average taxpayer in this country. Particularly if they would allow greater exemptions up to the $5,000 a year wage earner it would give immediate relief.
The budget is deceptive because in it there appears to be a great deal but in reality it gives very little. Its augmentation of the pay cheque of the average worker will scarcely be noticed. It is also an insincere budget because it enters the field of deficit budgeting in order to take care of a condition the existence of which the government denies. It will lengthen the life of the inflationary situation in which we are living and which has such a dire effect on the living costs of those who are on fixed incomes.
The government should be ashamed of themselves for the plight in which they have placed these people. They have allowed inflation to take place; they have allowed prices to rise and spiral. Everyone else has been in the position where they have had their wages

increased and have had allowances made to them, whereas these people must subsist on what they were expected by this government to live on some 10 or 15 years ago. True, there has been a little added, even to the soldier's pension. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) probably summed it up right when he said, "A little more for the soldier"; just a little and that is all.
Of course we all know that it is too soon to expect alluring programs of continued prosperity, pie in the sky and job security. These things must wait for an election year. The taxpayers know by now that they cannot expect these things at present because it is too soon for the promise of an improvement in financial conditions that will be offered as bait for votes. Probably that promise will come next year. We can hope it may be next year. For the sake of the people of this country I hope it is. However, financially the budget itself is a dud.
Everyone is anxious that our economy shall continue to expand. While the economy is now in an apparently healthy condition, this condition will not continue unless business expansion accompanies it. Such an expansion will spur a general activity which will create new employment. The reappearance of unemployment every year can no longer be regarded as of only temporary concern in view of its increasing proportions and lengthening periods. The recurrence of unemployment every year is extremely ominous.
Everyone seems to indulge, year after year, in giving a name to the budget. Some call it an alluring one. Some call it ambidextrous because one hand does not know what the other hand is doing. I think the hon. member for Eglinton started out by saying that it was a budget of crumbs. He probably made a mistake and should have said that it was a crummy budget. I probably would accept the Minister of Finance's own description of it. An article appeared in the Telegram of April 16, when the furor took place about the other convention that was being held and some reference was made to Trotskyites or something like that. I do not know the interpretation of these academic questions. I read the article and after I read it I said to myself, "This is an amazing statement to come from the Minister of Finance", so I read it again. The article reads in part as follows :
The Finance Minister called his recent budget "a pain, ordinary Liberal budget," not "a fantasy of imagination or a stand-pat budget."
I think everyone will agree that it is a pain budget because everybody in the country has a pain from it or is going to get a pain
The Budget-Mr. Small from it sooner or later. As he said, it certainly is not a fantasy of imagination, because if you have a pain, there is certainly no fantasy about it and it is not imaginary. It is not a stand-pat budget-and again he has aptly described it-because if you have a pain, you do not stand pat; you do something about it. I therefore think we will probably let the budget go at the Minister of Finance's own interpretation of it, namely that it is a pain, ordinary Liberal budget.
I probably could go a little bit further with the Minister of Finance. The other day he was speaking to a luncheon club and made some reference to the coming provincial election, particularly to Premier Frost's 14 points that he had read in the newspapers. He said he was "astonished" at the premier's claim that his government was responsible for old age pensions at the age of 70 without a means test, and he wondered when one starts to rewrite history. The Minister of Finance ought to know that very well, because that is all the Liberal party have been doing during their existence. They have been rewriting the policies of the Conservative party ever since confederation. Not only that, but they have revamped many of the Conservative party's policies, have filched them from their niche of proven worth and time-honoured tradition and then have masqueraded them in a cloak of simulated free trade. What a predicament!
While I am at it, let me just say this to the pesky lot of free traders over there who ever since confederation have deluded the people by adopting all the protective policies which the Conservative party introduced in this country, disguising them or dressing them up, and then parading under them as if they were free trade policies. The references made by the Minister of Finance the other day when he was outlining a few of the outstanding finance ministers who had functioned in this great dominion and who did yeoman service, brought back to my mind certain things which happened and which cause one to do a little bit of thinking.
The minister mentioned the great finance ministers of the Liberal party since confederation. He also went on to mention some of the finance ministers of the Conservative party. One stood out in his mind and stands out in mine, because for a while I thought the day of political and intellectual honesty had departed. But here was a man who, because of his strong convictions at the time of the reciprocity campaign, left his party. Because he was conscientious, had firm convictions and a grasp of the circumstances of the situation he left his party and came over to the Conservative party.

The Budget-Mr. Small
The situation was repeated when the conscription issue was before the country in 1917. There was some soul-searching taking place, and there were those who walked from the government side of the house to the opposition side and those who crossed from the opposition side to the government side. They were showing the calibre of men there were in those days. Indeed, one does not like to see dissension taking place in any party or turmoil raising its ugly head in any organization, but it was heartening to see the action of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) when he came to the decision a while ago, in good faith, that he must come to a parting of the ways with his party. I said to myself, surely this is a return to the days when conscience possessed each member and they could not live with themselves unless they did the honest thing.
I hope there will be a return to probity of conduct when each one will follow the policies he feels in his heart he should support, when there will no longer be any camouflage in this house or in the country. I said to myself, well, I guess others have offered up a prayer with me that honesty shall prevail.
In the short time I have been in the house I have listened to individual members on the government side stand up and give voice to utterances that are nothing but pure Conservative doctrine and policy of protection. They talk about the Conservative party all the time as the high protection party, but they only want for the nation protection that will give work to our citizens, that will keep them working and keep the wheels of industry turning. Surely this is the time there should be a grand exodus from the government side of the house to this side, because if these members were honest with themselves over 40 per cent of them would be over here with us fighting for the things their people need, and not hiding behind a simulated free trade cloak that is nothing more than protection. They are all giving vent, in some shape or form, to some protectionist policy or protective idea for the good of their ridings or for the good of the country, and eventually the Liberal party will be found out.
There is something in Abraham Lincoln's statement years ago that you may fool some of the people all the time and all the people some of the time, but you will not fool all the people all of the time. I think the day is near at hand when the people will waken up to what the Liberal government is doing to this great dominion. I should like to review a few of the things that have been done by
[Mr. Small.!
the Conservative party, not necessarily by the federal party but also by the party provincially. The reason I do so is that the Toronto Daily Star had an article a few days ago headed, "Mr. Frost Steals the Credit", which reads in part as follows:
Three of Mr. Frost's 1955 election planks are old age pensions, housing and the St. Lawrence waterway.
The article goes on to say that the federal government was responsible for these things. Mr. Frost is not stealing the St. Lawrence waterway, national housing or old age pensions. These all had their genesis in the Conservative party.

I suppose you will be delighted to hear that the national housing scheme, for which you take so much credit, germinated in the fertile brain of Tommy Church. You can laugh that one off too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let me cover the situation as far as the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned. This undertaking was not brought about overnight by the government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has been there a long time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I remind you that the fight for this project was commenced about the same time as the hydro project in Ontario, over 50 years ago. It was a Conservative government in the province of Ontario that kept it alive. There were a goodly number of conscientious Liberals identified with it from time to time, but the outstanding

protagonist of the project in those years was Adam Beck. At that time the Evening Telegram was the most outstanding proponent of public ownership through its brilliant editor, John Robinson, and its owner, John Ross Robertson. They kept the campaign going over the years, and associated with it were Joe Oliver, Tom Foster, Tommy Church, Reg. Geary, Alf. McGuire, Tom Han-nigan from Guelph and a number of other individuals from the United States, whose names I have forgotten for the moment, who were greatly interested in the deep-sea waterway.
The power barons in Montreal were most desirous of seeing that the project did not come to fruition. Through years of frustration these people carried on the fight. It was very discouraging, but finally those in the province of Quebec, who thought their interests were going to be hurt, decided they would throw in their lot, making it possible to reach an agreement. Then came the lobbyists in the United States who were determined that the seaway would not be built. The only reason the project is going ahead today is that we have to have the iron ore of Ungava transported through the seaway and across the great lakes to replace the high-class iron ore that has been exhausted in the United States Mesabi range. That is the only reason the St. Lawrence seaway is being constructed today. If you want to know why it is coming into being the reason is the efforts of Conservative governments in the province of Ontario under James Whitney, William Hearst, Howard Ferguson, George Henry, George Drew and Leslie Frost. They are the ones who should get the credit for the seaway. That is a basic fact. They can take the credit for it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A stout effort.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think you should refrain from sticking your neck out any farther. Let me read you an editorial appearing in the Toronto Daily Star of July 25, 1944:
On December 22. 1942, Mr. John Bracken made his radio debut as leader of the Progressive Conservative party. Said Mr. Bracken; "Every human being that is born into our society has a right to feel that he is welcome in it . . . and that, in the event of old age, ill-health or other misfortune overtaking him, he will have the assurance of a reasonable standard of social and economic security."
In the following February, the Progressive Conservative leader made another speech in which he declared: "The human family is our greatest asset. There are 11,500,000 human souls in Canada. Some come into the world handicapped from the beginning. Many grow up ill-nourished. Some die at an early age. It is reported that there are a third of a million sick on the average every day, and that the sick bill comes to $300 million a year. We have made a poor job of conserving and developing our human resources. We must increase the preventive services. We must make ours a race of healthy and efficient men and women."
These and many similar statements which Mr. Bracken has made in the period which has since elapsed are in accordance with the purpose which was allegedly to be served by reforming the old Conservative party. It was to become progressive. It was to favour "a reasonable standard of social and economic security". It was to support social service measures. Well, it has now the opportunity to support two of these-children's allowances and a national health service.
I want you to get this.
But Conservative papers are already fearful about the cost, and there are indications that the party will oppose one or both of these bills in parliament.
Who is worrying about the cost? Is it the Conservative party that is worrying about the cost? Neither we nor any other party in the house except the Liberals are worrying about the cost.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You sing a different tune when the matter is laid on your own doorstep. More than that, you have been sailing this Liberal scow with the chart that was given to you by William Lyon Mackenzie King in 1919 when he espoused, as one of the planks in his platform, a national health

The Budget-Mr. Henderson program. The clipping from which I have quoted was dated 1944, about 11 years ago, and the statement was made that the Conservative party would probably be opposed because of the cost. Yet 11 years later the government is singing the same old song, it is going to cost too much money. We could have told them that then, but they are waking up 11 years later to the fact that this is going to cost the taxpayers of Canada a lot of money. When will you get some sense and let a party that knows how run the country?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am quite sure the hon. member for Danforth would have been very pleased if he could sing words of praise as a result of tax decreases levied in the 1954 Ontario budget. I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance on the fine budget he has presented to this house. I might say that his record showed that he was a master at deriving sound results, and he has not let us down with his first budget.
My remarks will take a very short time tonight, and I should like to direct them in support of those men and women who are employed in the penitentiaries of Canada. I should like to support their request for the five-day 40-hour week. I might say that I am not alone in giving this my support. I am sure my remarks are in accord with the opinion of the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir). He has spent a great deal of time investigating matters and putting forth his ideas. He has joined me in all the work I could do on behalf of these employees. I might say also that I appreciate the assistance which has been given to me by the amalgamated civil servants of Canada and more particularly the local representative at Kingston, Mr. Reid.
Referring to the situation in Kingston alone, may I say that it affects 350 employees at the Kingston penitentiary, Collins Bay and the women's penitentiary. It is not limited to the employees alone but affects the husbands and wives of these employees. As I understand government policy, it is that civil servants are given a five-day 40-hour week in areas where the five-day 40-hour week is prevalent in industry. This is the case in the city of Kingston in so far as industry and the larger companies are concerned. Civil servants in other departments in that city have been granted these working conditions.
I must admit that the Department of Justice has a problem on its hands, because these penitentiary officers are dealing with
[Mr. Small.1

human beings. I suggest for these reasons that the type of men we need as guards, and which we have been fortunate in getting, are men of good character, alert, considerate and able to stand tension. In order to get this type of individual to work as a guard in the penitentiary we must be able to at least compete and have equivalent working conditions with other kinds of employment.
These men who work as guards and in other positions in the penitentiaries are working under hazardous conditions, and under great tension. As a result of tests it has been shown that the greatest cause of sickness and death amongst the employees of penitentiaries has been hypertension. This is another reason why these employees should have long periods of relaxation.
In order to put the five-day 40-hour week into effect I realize that additional employees would be required, with the resultant additional expenditure of funds. You cannot lock up human beings over the week end and let everybody go home. It has been suggested to me that there might be a shorter work week, without the inmates being locked up for additional time, if the shops were closed on Saturday morning, housekeeping activities such as haircutting, baths and clothing changes could be effected, and Saturday afternoon and Sunday left for recreational purposes. With a system of alternating the essential officers and increases in the number of custodial officers only, a shorter work week could be put into effect. Another point would be that the five-day 40-hour week would result in happy, contented guards, and I am quite sure this system would bring about, indirectly, the rehabilitation of the inmates. I am quite sure that happy, contented guards would impart the same feeling to the inmates of the penitentiary.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I appeal for the five-day 40-hour week for the penitentiary employees. I might conclude by saying that would be most difficult for any member of this house to explain to the wife and family of a guard, whose job is tense and hazardous and Who cannot spend two days out of seven at home, why the man next door, who is employed at a desk job by another department of government, is able to spend two days out of seven at home with his wife and family. I hope this suggestion will obtain some results.
I wish to adjourn the debate, Mr. Speaker.
On motion of Mr. Henderson the debate was adjourned.
